Install Usage Architecture Building README

What it does

  • Opens a folder of rasters (1 file = 1 date), a multiband file (1 band = 1 date), a list of files or a wildcard pattern. Dates are parsed from file names or band descriptions (YYYY-MM-DD, YYYYMMDD, YYYY_MM, YYYY, A2001001, ...). A multiband file holding several bands a date, date after date, opens as such (each date of several bands, see below) when its bands are named <date>_<band> (2020-01-15_red, as Zeit's save_raster writes a time x band stack), or when a <name>_dates.csv next to it (a date a row, from the column named Date, as Zeit and cdts write it) has one date for every few bands: 875 bands and 125 dates are 7 bands a date, named Band 1 to Band 7 without names in the file. With a date for every band it dates a file of one band a date. A file whose bands have wavelengths (hyperspectral, e.g. EnMAP) opens as a spectrum (see Spectra). A file whose bands each have a name that is not a date opens as a stack of variables: each band a map of its own (its own stretch and classes), picked by name over the map instead of played; no temporal statistics, trends or series chart, the value of every band under the cursor in Statistics (Display → A stack of variables switches it).
  • Categorical series (land cover, masks, classifications): detected when the file has a colour table, category names or an attribute table, or when a date has only a few whole values. Each class gets the file's colour (or one of a qualitative palette) and name, editable in a legend; the chart shows the class sequence as steps with class names on the axis, and the statistics show the class at the date, the majority class, the number of changes and the last change (e.g. 2006: Forest → Pasture).
  • Several bands per date (e.g. one Landsat surface-reflectance file per date): show any band or a normalized difference of two (NDVI, NDMI, NBR...), and hide cloudy observations with a quality band (Fmask codes, Landsat Collection 2 QA_PIXEL bits or a 0/1 mask; a band named Fmask or QA_PIXEL is used automatically). Multiband tools such as CCDC read every band. The map can show three bands of each date as an RGB composite (true colour, colour infrared...) while the chart keeps the band or index.
  • Map modes, all computed on the GPU: value at date, anomaly (value − mean), difference (value − a reference date: a fixed date or the previous one), temporal mean, standard deviation, linear trend (OLS, per year), minimum, maximum, amplitude, trend R², largest drop (date and magnitude of the largest decrease between consecutive valid observations) and a multitemporal RGB of three dates. Changing date, colormap or stretch is instant; there is an animation player.
  • Pixel series: approximate (from the overview) as soon as you hover, exact (full resolution) once the mouse rests. Click to drop pins and compare pixels; Shift+drag a rectangle for an ROI, or draw a polygon (R: click its vertices or drag a freehand outline; or Alt + click a polygon of a vector layer): mean and p10–p90 per date, a box plot per date (p25–p75 box, median, whiskers to p10 and p90), a fan (p10–p90 and p25–p75 bands, the median dashed) or the density of every pixel's value at each date (two groups of pixels, a half-cleared plot, show as two bands where the mean runs between them), of the pixels whose centres are inside.
  • Chart: from the first date to the last; lines, markers, stems, stairs or bars (from the mean, or from 0 for anomalies, in the map's anomaly colours below and above it); raw values, anomaly, z-score, seasonal anomaly (each value minus the mean of its calendar month over every year: the seasonal cycle taken out, a drought stands out) or CUSUM (the running sum of the anomalies: a change of slope is a change of level); OLS or Sen trend line per series; Y axis locked to the map range if you want; stripes under the chart (a colour per date of the cursor's, the ROI's or the last pin's series, as the map colours it).
  • Statistics per series: n, mean, median, std, CV, min/max (with date), amplitude, OLS slope + R², Sen's slope, largest drop (with date) and, in the difference mode, the difference shown on the map (the Mann-Kendall test, with autocorrelation corrections, is a Zeit tool).
  • Pixel values: when the active layer is not a series shown (hidden, a single image, a stack of bands), or a run's map is shown over it (a class map just made over its series: the view follows the layer on top; a tool's preview aside), the chart's panel becomes Pixel values: a row per layer the map shows (the maps of the runs, single images, the other series at their dates), top of the drawing order first, with its value under the cursor and at each pin (a class by its name, a year as a year; * while a series' value is still from its overview), Copy as tab-separated text. A row clicked (here, or in Layers) is described: its histogram beside the table in the map's colours, the cursor and the pins marked on it; in Statistics, its pixels with a value and their area (hectares, on a projected CRS), minimum, maximum, mean, standard deviation and percentiles, and, for whole numbers (classes, years), its pixels, percentage and hectares by value (LandTrendr's year of detection: the area of each year's loss). Show the series again: the chart comes back.
  • Full resolution on zoom: past the overview resolution, tiles of the visible area are read in the background and cached on the GPU (value and difference modes; the difference reads the tiles of both dates).
  • Full-resolution cache: a lossless copy of the whole series in the cache folder (an SSD), built in the background; exact series, pins, ROI and detail tiles are then read from it, about 1 ms per series even when the files sit on a spinning HDD. On by default for series on an HDD (see Performance).
  • Fast: about 0.15 s from launch to the first frame; the app sleeps when nothing changes (a frame costs ~0.3 ms of CPU). The cube overview is cached on disk, so reopening a series takes a fraction of a second.
  • Export: the map as a PNG figure (as shown, rendered at 1×, 2× or 4× the screen resolution, with the date, a colour bar or class legend, pins and the ROI if wanted, on the map's, a white or a transparent background); the active layer's values at the date as a Float32 GeoTIFF (visible area or whole image, full resolution, same grid and CRS, no data = NaN) and the rendered view as an RGBA GeoTIFF, both ready for QGIS; Zeit results as GeoTIFF (e.g. each LandTrendr output: year of detection, magnitude, duration...); the embedding view shown (principal components, similarity, change) as a Float32 GeoTIFF at full resolution; a range of dates as an animation (GIF, or MP4/WebM through ffmpeg) with the date stamp, legend and a scale bar (see Animation). The export window shows where the file goes (Save to: type a path, or a name alone for the last export folder, or pick one with Browse...; it warns before replacing a file). Files are written in the background (File → Exports shows progress); Copy CSV of the cursor, pins and ROI series; Python...: code that reproduces a pin's or the ROI's series, its statistics and the Zeit tool on the chart, shown in the Python history's editor.
  • Layers: open several series at once (e.g. NDVI and NBR of the same area, or neighboring scenes). Layers are placed by their georeferencing, can be shown/hidden (including the first one), reordered and faded; the chart shows the series of the active layer or of every visible layer at the cursor/pins.
  • Layers in any CRS: a layer in another projection (e.g. UTM 22S next to UTM 23S, or geographic EPSG:4326 over UTM) or on a rotated grid is reprojected onto the active layer's grid on the GPU (nearest neighbour, values unchanged, error < 0.02 px). Cursor, pins and ROI use the exact PROJ transformation. The ROI applies to every visible layer.
  • Vector layers (File → Add vector layer, or drop them): field plots, samples, parcels... from GeoJSON, Shapefile, GeoPackage, KML, FlatGeobuf or a CSV of points, in any CRS, in one drawing order with the series (as in a GIS: a vector layer can go under a raster one). A polygon becomes the ROI with Alt + click; Extract series writes the series of every feature (a point's pixel, a polygon's mean) of the active or every visible layer to a CSV table. See Vector layers.
  • Interpretation (TimeSync style): go through a vector layer's features one by one (N / Shift+N), the map centred on each and its series on the chart, and label them with keys 1–9, a date of change (D) and notes; saved as you go and exported as GeoPackage, GeoJSON, Shapefile or CSV.
  • Basemap (Layers panel → Basemap): satellite imagery or a map under the series, for context. Sources: Esri World Imagery, Sentinel-2 cloudless 2016 by EOX (CC BY 4.0), OpenStreetMap, or your own XYZ URL (https://.../{z}/{x}/{y}.png?key=..., e.g. Google Map Tiles API, MapTiler, Planet: with your key and under the provider's terms). Off by default: nothing is downloaded until you pick a source, and each session and each series opened start with it hidden (the source is remembered; adding a layer keeps it) until you show it (its eye in the Layers panel). Only the tiles in view, at the screen's zoom level, are read in the background (coarser ones fill in while they arrive) and kept in the cache folder; the map never waits for them. It is drawn under every layer (lower a layer's opacity to see the ground), on the map panels and the swipe (whose comparison can be the basemap alone), and in the exports, always with the source's attribution (bottom right). Tiles are in Web Mercator and placed on the active layer's grid like a layer in another CRS, so the active layer needs a CRS. Offline, the map shows "Basemap unavailable (offline)".
  • Map panels side by side (View → New map view): each panel shows one layer, optionally at its own date and in its own display mode (e.g. NDVI next to NBR, or 2005 next to 2020 of the same series). All panels show the same area: pan or zoom in any of them moves every one; the cursor is mirrored as a cross, and pins and the ROI appear in all of them. Panels dock anywhere or go to another monitor; they share the loaded data (no extra memory).
  • Swipe (View → Swipe, C): a divider you drag across the map; left of it the map as it is, right of it another layer, or the same one at another date or in another display mode (picked in a bar above the map).
  • Space-time transect (Hovmöller): Ctrl + drag a line on the map (or T, then drag); the Transect panel shows distance along the line against the dates, in the layer's colours (class colours for categorical data), first from the overview and then at full resolution. Hover a cell for its distance, date and value (marked on the map), click to go to that date; values or anomalies; Copy CSV.

  • Analysis panel (View → Analysis), its tabs:

    • Dates: the visible area at every date side by side (or the dates of the shown date's month, every year), in the layer's colours (Value at date: its colormap and range, or its classes), each with its date and the share of it that is valid; valid at least keeps only the clean dates, size the small maps' width. A click goes to the date. Clouds, gaps and a change are seen at once. Made from the overview, again as the map moves.
    • Seasonal (series with several dates a year): the cursor, a pin or the ROI mean by day of the year, one line per year (colour = year, the current date's year on top) with the mean of all years by month (± 1 standard deviation), or a year × day-of-year heatmap in the layer's colours; the year can start in any month (Year from: July, a southern summer's crop from October to March seen whole; years named 2019/20).
    • Classes (categorical layers): the share of each class at every date (stacked areas or lines) and the transitions between two dates (the largest ones, the share of pixels that changed, the full matrix); Copy CSV of both. Flows: a Sankey diagram between two to six dates across the panel's width, or Open in a window for one as large as you make it (a bar per class as tall as its pixels, a few points at least; a ribbon per change shaded from the class it left to the one it joined, the pixels that kept their class fainter; the outer columns named with their shares; hover for the rest), counted a pair of consecutive dates at a time. Other < 0.5% groups the classes under that share at every date (0.5 to 5%, or none) as one grey class, its tooltip naming them. Changes only leaves out the pixels that kept their class: only what changed, at a scale of its own (a class that changed nowhere disappears). The wheel zooms on the pointer (up to 40x), a drag moves the diagram, a double click (or Fit) shows it whole; the names follow the part of each bar in view.
    • Scatter: two layers, or two dates of one, pixel by pixel in the ROI (or the whole image) as a density plot, with the 1:1 line, the least squares line, r, R², the mean difference and its RMS; the trajectory of the cursor, a pin or the ROI mean between the two layers date by date (coloured by time, arrows the way it goes: a season's loop, a disturbance and its recovery).
    • Trend test: whether the trend of a region (the ROI, the visible area or the whole image), or of each class of a categorical layer, differs from 0, and whether the classes' trends differ, by PARTS (Ives et al. 2021, the R package remotePARTS): each pixel's AR(1) trend, the spatial correlation of the pixels fitted to their residuals, and a GLS of the trends in random partitions of the pixels, combined into tests that account for the correlation between partitions. The table gives each mean trend with its standard error, t and p, the chi-square test of the classes, and, for comparison, how many pixels' own tests are significant (which is no regional test: neighbours are correlated, and thousands of tests run at once). Runs on a thread (seconds to a minute), reading the region at full resolution (one pixel in k × k of a large one); Copy CSV. A guide with screenshots, the method step by step and how to read the results: Trend test.
    • Areas: the area of each class at every date of the active series, or of each value of a run's map (a map of change years counted by year, a map of lengths of time in years, such as LandTrendr's duration, by whole years: 0-1, 1-2...; Area by value... in its menu), on the ROI or the whole layer, counted at full resolution in a task (Count; also Areas... in Classes). Each pixel has its true area: the geotransform's in an equal-area projection, else its geodesic area on the CRS's ellipsoid (longitudes and latitudes by latitude; UTM and other projections by their scale, the note saying how far the nominal pixel area is from it, e.g. +0.05%). Bars per date (the classes stacked) or per value in ha, km² or %, a table of a date (pixels, ha, km², %), Copy / Save CSV, and areas.csv written in the task's folder. The mapped area: Validation gives the adjusted one with its interval.
    • Zonal: the last Zonal statistics over time run (a vector layer's menu) drawn for one feature: the mean and median over the dates with the bands from the 10th to the 90th and the 25th to the 75th percentile, or the area of each class stacked by date (of each year, a map of change dates). The feature picked in the attribute table is followed.

    Classes and scatter count the overview's pixels (what the map shows before zooming in), so they are immediate on any series.

  • Files panel: a folder tree listing only rasters by default; double click opens a series as a new layer, right click adds it as a layer or to Favorites (listed on top, kept between sessions). A folder's tooltip says what it would open as ("41 rasters, 1985 to 2025, yearly", from the file names). Whatever is opened (from the panel, File → Open, a drop or the command line), the tree goes to it. Whatever is opened joins the map as a new layer, as in a GIS (File → Close all starts again); dropping several files with Shift held makes each one a layer of its own (File → Open files as separate layers... too), without it they make one series. In Layers, a series unfolded lists its dates: one dragged out of it becomes a layer of its own and the series is opened again without it; the series' menu Split into layers makes every date a layer of its own, in a group named after the series, to show several at once. Either way the new layers take the series' colours (its ranges and class names too).
  • Detachable panels: drag any panel out of the main window, e.g. the map on a second monitor and the charts on the first.
  • Settings (File → Settings, Ctrl+,): a colour theme (dark, light, classic, Janus, Studio, Graphite or Matrix), translucent panels or a translucent window (the desktop shows through), the interface font size, and how many CPU threads Janus and Zeit may use (all cores but 2 by default, so the computer stays responsive during long runs).
  • Zeit tools (Zeit change detection and time-series algorithms): LandTrendr, Mann-Kendall (with Sen's slope; Hamed-Rao, Yue-Wang and seasonal variants), the AR(1) trend (remotePARTS's REML fit: a t-test of the trend that accounts for the series' autocorrelation, what the Trend test tests over a region), emerging hot spots (the Getis-Ord Gi* of every date and the Mann-Kendall trend of each pixel's Gi*: ESRI's patterns, new, consecutive, intensifying, persistent, diminishing, sporadic, oscillating or historical hot or cold spot; the Gi* equals R sfdep's), BFAST, BFAST Lite, BFAST Monitor, phenology (season start/peak/end, length, amplitude), CCDC (multiband), CODED (forest degradation, multiband), the NDFI (spectral unmixing), Tmask (clouds the quality band missed), TWDTW classification (classes from pins), SOM and k-means clustering (typical trajectories, named by the samples in them), SNIC segmentation (segments of alike trajectories, with their polygons), the agreement of several change maps and smoothing (Whittaker, Savitzky-Golay; chart only). Each is fitted live on the cursor, pins and ROI series (segments, trend lines, break dates, seasons or CCDC models drawn on the chart), or run on the whole image, the visible area or an ROI, with the results (year of detection, magnitude, slope, p-value, break dates...) shown as map layers; the NDFI and the series screened by Tmask open as new layers. Zeit's methods are part of Janus — nothing to install, no Python.

Command line

jn [options] [input ...]

Inputs:
  folder\             every raster in the folder, 1 file = 1 date
  series.tif          1 multiband file, 1 band = 1 date
  a.tif b.tif ...     several files, 1 file = 1 date
  "ndvi_*.tif"        wildcard pattern (* and ?)
  https://.../cog.tif cloud-optimized GeoTIFFs on the web, read in place (only
  s3://, gs://, az:// the blocks shown are downloaded); several URLs = a series
  clim.nc, data.zarr  NetCDF / Zarr / HDF: a variable's time steps (CF dates);
                      with several variables the window asks which one, or
                      name it: NETCDF:"clim.nc":t2m, ZARR:"data.zarr":/t2m
  plots.gpkg ...      vector files (GeoJSON, Shapefile, GeoPackage, KML, CSV
                      of points) open as vector layers over the series
  work.janus          a project: its layers, styles, view and the rest, as saved

Options:
  --band N            band used when each file is one date (default: 1)
  --budget MB         memory for the cube overview, this run only
                      (default: Settings, 1024)
  --threads N         processing threads, this run only (default: Settings);
                      with --selftest-zeit, Zeit's threads
  --full-res off|hdd|all  the full-resolution cache, this run only (default: Settings): on demand,
                      for series on an HDD, for every series
  -h, --help          show this help
  --version           show the version

Developer options (all of them in jn --help):
  --describe IN       print how IN opens (dates, size, CRS, variables of a
                      NetCDF / Zarr, the series of the centre pixel) and exit
  --profile-tour IN   a fixed tour of IN (overview, cursor series, dates, modes,
                      zoom and pan at full resolution, an ROI), timed stage by stage
  --measure-cache on|off IN  time exact series and ROI from the files, build the
                      overview (and the full-resolution cache if on), time the
                      reads again from the cache
  --selftest-zeit IN  run the Zeit tools end to end on IN without a window
  --selftest-validation  check the sampling design, strata, sample and accuracy
                      estimators (Olofsson et al. 2014)
  --selftest-ui A B [C [D [E [F [G]]]]]  drive the interface frame by frame on
                      the series of tools/make_selftest_data.py
  --shots TOUR IN OUT  a website guide's screenshots (PNGs in OUT): validation,
                      landtrendr, ccdc, coded, bfast, phenology

Examples:

jn D:\data\ndvi_annual\
jn landsat_stack.tif
jn "S2_*_NDVI.tif" --band 1
jn https://sentinel-cogs.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/sentinel-s2-l2a-cogs/36/Q/WD/2020/7/S2A_36QWD_20200701_0_L2A/B04.tif
jn era5_t2m.nc
jn NETCDF:"cmip6.nc":tas --band 3     (the 3rd level of a variable with levels)

jn opens the window and returns the prompt immediately (on Windows jn.com is a small console launcher next to janus.exe, the same trick Visual Studio uses with devenv.com; the one on PATH is in the install folder's bin, alone, so that Janus's DLLs stay out of other programs' way).

MCP server

janus mcp (or jn mcp) makes Janus a server of the Model Context Protocol on its standard input and output: an assistant (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, any MCP client) works with your series through Janus's own engines, without the window and without Python. Every result is a file (cloud-optimized GeoTIFFs, VRTs, CSVs, .janusmodel), in the folder the call names or under Janus's results folder (results/mcp/<tool>_<time>); its paths are in the answer. Long calls report their progress and stop when the client cancels them. --threads N caps the processing threads (default: Settings').

ToolWhat it does
describe_seriesa series' size, CRS, pixel size, extent (also in longitude and latitude), bands, dates, what is shown
list_indicesthe spectral indices by name, with their formulas
pixel_seriesthe values of places through time (pixels, coordinates or longitude and latitude; other bands too)
region_serieseach date's statistics of an area (valid share, mean, std, min, p10, median, p90, max); sampled when large
check_expressiona raster calculator text planned over named layers: the result (dates or an image), grid, layers read, or the error's line and column
calculatethe text computed: a COG per date (or VRTs computed when read)
list_tools, describe_toolZeit's tools, their parameters and outputs
run_toola Zeit tool on a series or an area of it (BFAST, CCDC, LandTrendr, trends, phenology...); TWDTW from samples (each class's mean series its pattern); the SOM's and k-means' clusters named by the samples' classes; the tools on maps (agreement of change maps) on maps
regularizea fixed step (16 days, month, year): median, medoid or clearest date, gaps filled
specklea radar series through Quegan's multitemporal filter or Lee's
harmonizeSentinel-2 taken to Landsat 8's OLI by HLS's bandpass adjustment (Landsat 7 and 4-5 by Roy et al. 2016 if asked); with join, a second series on the same grid joined in time
warpa raster reprojected, resampled, clipped (gdalwarp)
zonaleach polygon's statistics, or areas of each class or change year, of maps; a CSV
areasthe area of each class or change year of maps (each pixel's own area); a CSV
polygonizea map of classes or dates into polygons (a GeoPackage), small patches merged, simplified
rasterizea vector layer on a raster's or a series' grid: 1 inside, each feature's number or an attribute
train_classifiera Random Forest, TempCNN, L-TAE, Presto (a year's dates, fine-tuned) or U-TAE (patches of the area, on PASTIS's weights or none) on samples (places with a class, or a vector file and its class field), validated (by place for the forest)
classifya .janusmodel applied to a series or an area: class map, probability, area of applicability
stac_catalogsthe STAC catalogues Janus knows (Earth Search, Planetary Computer, ...) and their collections
stac_searcha collection's items over an area and dates (and cloud cover): the dates found, the clouds of each, the bands to choose
stac_seriesthe search as a series: VRTs read in place, downloaded (a cloud-optimized GeoTIFF a date) or composited (best available pixel, greenest, medoid or median, the whole range or a year a period); clouds masked by the quality band
describe_vectora vector file's layers: features, geometry, CRS, extent (also in longitude and latitude), fields, the first features
vector_serieseach feature's series (a point's pixel, a polygon's mean) of a series; a CSV of feature, id, date, value and pixels
open_in_janusfiles shown in Janus, places as pins: as layers of the window already open (it comes to the front; it watches an inbox beside Janus's data), else in a new window

A series is a path (a folder, a file, a wildcard) or {"paths": [...], "band": 4, "expression": "NDVI", "qa_band": 7}; a place is {"col", "row"}, {"x", "y"} (the series' CRS) or {"lon", "lat"}; an area a window in pixels, a bbox in the CRS or a bbox_lonlat.

Claude Code:

claude mcp add janus -- "C:\Program Files\Janus\janus.exe" mcp --threads 8

Claude Desktop (claude_desktop_config.json):

json
{ "mcpServers": { "janus": { "command": "C:\\Program Files\\Janus\\janus.exe", "args": ["mcp", "--threads", "8"] } } }

Using the window

ActionHow
Remote rasters (cloud)File → Open URL... (Ctrl+U, a new layer): one URL per line, several make a series. https://, s3://, gs://, az://: cloud-optimized GeoTIFFs (AWS Earth Search, Planetary Computer with a signed URL, USGS, ESA...) are read in place through GDAL's network file systems: only the header, the overview level the map needs and the blocks looked at (the cursor's pixel, the detail tiles) are downloaded. Public S3 and GCS buckets need no account; private ones use the usual credentials (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, ~/.aws, GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS, AZURE_STORAGE_CONNECTION_STRING...). Dates come from the file names, or from the folder each file sits in (Sentinel-2 COGs: .../S2B_23KPQ_20230811_0_L2A/B04.tif). The overview is cached on disk like any other
Build a seriesFile → Build series...: loose files (picked, or a folder's) grouped by the date in their names (as when opening); a date's files of one band stacked as its bands (their names from what tells the files apart: S2_20210105_T1_B04 and ..._B08 give B04 and B08), its tiles (files of other extents) mosaicked; files of several bands each keep their bands. Every date on one grid (the files' extent at their finest pixel; one CRS: files of another are left out, reproject them first). The plan is shown before anything is written: the dates, each band's files and tiles, the files left out and why. Then a folder of VRTs (gdalbuildvrt's own code: at once, nothing copied) or of COGs, <name>_<YYYYMMDD>, opened as a series (a task; its provenance kept)
Save a seriesFile → Save series as...: the active series, the quantity shown (a band, an index or an expression, its quality mask applied) or, for NetCDF and Zarr, every band (a variable each), over the whole layer, the visible area or the ROI, as a multiband COG (a band per date, its date in the band's name: it opens back as a series), a NetCDF (CF: time in days since 1970, x / y or lon / lat, the CRS as a grid mapping) or a Zarr with a time axis; opened back when saved (a task). Reprojected or clipped by polygons: Tools → Data preparation → Reproject, resample, clip first
STAC catalogsFile → Search STAC catalog...: Earth Search (Sentinel-2 Collection 1 L2A), Planetary Computer (Sentinel-2 L2A, Landsat Collection 2 L2, HLS S30 and L30, Sentinel-1 RTC), Brazil Data Cube (16-day cubes of Sentinel-2, Landsat, CBERS-4 WFI) or another STAC API by its URL (List all gives its collections). The visible area, the ROI or a box in degrees, two dates and the maximum cloud cover; Search lists the dates found with their scenes and clouds (Clearest ticks those under 10%), then the bands (with their wavelengths; SCL and QA_PIXEL as the quality band) and the cell size. Open as a layer writes one VRT per date (the mosaic of the day's scenes, the clearest on top, on one grid: the CRS of most scenes, the finest band's cells; scenes of another UTM zone warped onto it) under results/stac and opens them, read in place; Download as GeoTIFFs writes the same series as cloud-optimized GeoTIFFs (Tools → Tasks). Planetary Computer's files are read with tokens Janus asks for and renews, also when the folder is opened again later. Sentinel-1 RTC (radar, VV and VH as linear gamma0 corrected for the terrain, 10 m; no clouds to filter, no quality band): the search lists the satellite's passes (ascending or descending, relative orbit) and keeps the one with the most scenes (Pass; mixing passes makes false steps), and the series opens in dB (the VVdB index, 10 * log10(VV); VHdB and VHVVdB, the ratio, and the radar indices of the library in the Display panel); Tools → Data preparation → Speckle filter smooths it. Composite: one image of the dates ticked (or one a year) instead of the series, written as cloud-optimized GeoTIFFs and opened as a layer (a task): the best available pixel (each pixel's clear observation of the highest score, every band from that date: its day of the year near a target day (exp(-0.5 (days / ±)²), the middle of the dates unless typed as MM-DD), its distance to the nearest cloud or shadow of its date (0 at the first distance or nearer, 1 at the second or farther: 30 to 1500 m by default), its sensor (Landsat 7 after its scan line corrector failed in 2003: 0.5) and its scene's cloud cover, weighted 0.3, 0.5, 0.1 and 0.1; Griffiths et al. 2013, White et al. 2014; zeit's build_annual_composites(method="bap")), the greenest (the highest NDVI, Earth Engine's qualityMosaic), the medoid or the median. The best available pixel reads the quality band of every date first, in blocks of 1024 pixels with the margin of the cloud distance around them, chooses the winners, then reads the bands of the dates that win in each block only, each over the box of its winners there (and a pixel's next best date where a winner has a band without a value): most of a series is never downloaded (the job's log says how many pixels were read of those every date's bands would need); the greenest reads the red, NIR and quality bands of every date; the medoid and the median every band. The date, score and clear observations of each pixel adds a GeoTIFF per composite in its info folder (year, day of the year, score, clear dates). --stac-composite bap|greenest|medoid|median[;yearly] with --stac. HLS's Fmask is a quality rule of its own (HLS Fmask bits: cloud, adjacent, shadow and snow masked). Footprints as a vector layer: the scenes' outlines with their id, date and cloud cover. See the STAC guide
NetCDF, Zarr, HDFopen the file (or the .zarr folder): with several variables a list asks which one (name, shape, long name and units); the time axis is decoded from CF units (days since 1970-01-01, hours, months...) and calendars (noleap, 360_day, all_leap...: a model's 30 February becomes the 28th/29th); hourly data are labelled with the hour. Display panel → Variable: another variable of the file, level: another value of the other dimensions (pressure level, depth, member); both reopen the layer in place. A lon/lat grid without a grid mapping is taken as WGS 84
Pan / zoomdrag / mouse wheel (zooming out goes as far as the CRS's area of use and every layer, the basemap under all of it; zooming in until the finest layer in view, active or not, shows its pixels as large as the active one's may be, each drawn from its full-resolution tiles, not only its overview), F fits the active layer; trackpad: two fingers pan, pinch zooms
Pixel serieshover (exact once the mouse rests)
Command paletteCtrl+K (or Ctrl+Shift+P; View → Command palette): type what you want (bfast, evi, swipe, export png, a layer's name): the menus' commands, every tool, the display modes, the spectral indices the active layer has the bands for (shown on it), the open layers (make active, zoom to), the panels, and the features of the vector layers with labels whose label holds what you type (any case; Go to feature: ..., up to 50: the map moves to it, picked in the attribute table); each with its category and keys, the ones used last first; arrows and Enter, or a click; one that cannot run now is faint, the reason on hover. Esc or a click outside closes it
Go to a coordinateCtrl+G (View → Go to coordinate...): latitude and longitude in decimal degrees (-23.55, -46.63; a decimal comma works when no point is used: -23,55 -46,63), or in degrees, minutes and seconds with or without the hemisphere (23°33'S 46°38'W, 23 33 S 46 38 W, O for west too); UTM as zone + N/S (the hemisphere) or a latitude band (23S 333000 7394000, 23 K 333000 7394000); EPSG:code x y; two numbers past the degrees' range are x y in the layer's CRS; px column row a pixel. The window shows where it lands (the pixel, or that it is off the layer); Enter or Go centres the map there (zoomed in to a screen point a pixel at least) with a mark that fades, and Drop a pin there adds a pin. --goto PLACE on the command line
Saved viewsView → Saved views: a name and Save view keep the view (its centre in longitude and latitude and its width in metres, so any layer in any CRS goes back to the same area; a layer without a CRS: its pixels), the date shown and the layers shown; a click on one goes back to it (the date by its label, the layers shown by their names when any is open), x deletes it. Kept in the settings; also in the palette (Saved view: name)
MinimapM (View → Minimap): the active layer whole in the map's bottom right corner, the view as a rectangle on it; a click or a drag on it moves the map there. Drawn again only when what it shows changes. --minimap
LensL (View → Lens, or Lens on the swipe's bar): the swipe's comparison inside a circle that follows the cursor instead of right of a divider; Ctrl + wheel steps the date the lens shows (up: later; it takes its own date, as Own date on the bar) instead of zooming, the wheel alone zooms the map, Alt + wheel changes its size. L again turns it off (a swipe that was on before it, C, comes back as the divider). --lens
Status barat the foot of the window: under the cursor, the pixel (column, row), its coordinates in the layer's CRS and in longitude and latitude (WGS 84), and what the map shows there; at the right, the zoom, the map's scale on the screen (1:N at 96 points per inch) and the ground a screen pixel covers, the active layer's CRS, and the tasks under way (Zeit and deep-learning runs, downloads, exports) with the progress of the oldest: a click opens Tasks
Downloadsevery download runs in the background, the interface usable meanwhile: STAC series and composites, embeddings, the networks' weights (their megabytes said as they come). Each is a task in Tools → Tasks with its bar, its log and Cancel, and its bar on the map (top right); at most Downloads at once transfer at the same time (Settings, 2 by default), the others wait in line in the order they were asked for (waiting in Tasks, which says how many are before it; Move first makes one the next to start; the status bar counts those waiting). Two tasks needing the same weights or the AlphaEarth index download them once
Noticesa task that ends after a few seconds or more (or fails) leaves a notice at the bottom right: Show in Tasks, Open folder, Log; it goes after a few seconds (a failure stays longer) or with its ×. With Janus in the background, the system is asked for your attention (the taskbar's icon flashes; on a Mac, the Dock's bounces)
Compare pixelsclick to drop a pin
Close layersthe Layers panel: click a row to select it (a series also becomes active), Ctrl + click adds or takes a row, Shift + click selects the rows between; Delete or Ctrl+D (Mac: Command+D) closes the selected layers, series and vector layers alike (a row's menu: Close the N selected). The keys belong to the list until you click elsewhere
Remove a pinright click it (Mac: Control + click, or a two-finger click on the trackpad), Delete (last one) or the x in the statistics table
ROIShift + drag: rectangular ROI, mean and p10–p90 per date (or a box plot per date: the ROI list above the chart); with All visible layers on the chart, also on every visible layer (its own pixels under the rectangle, reprojected if needed)
Polygonal ROIR (or View → Draw ROI polygon), then click the vertices and close it on the first one, with a double click or Enter (Backspace undoes a vertex, Esc cancels); or, after R, drag a freehand outline (lasso), closed when you let go. The statistics, the local PCA of embeddings, the similarity to the ROI and the scatter use the pixels whose centres are inside; a Zeit run on the ROI covers its bounding box. Alt + click a polygon of a vector layer (holes included) to make it the ROI; View → Clear ROI
Edit ROI verticesShift+R (or View → Edit ROI vertices, the command palette) with an ROI, drawn or taken from a polygon of a vector layer (its file is not changed): a square at each vertex, a dot in the middle of each edge. Drag a vertex to move it; drag an edge's middle to add a vertex there; right click a vertex, or Delete / Backspace over it, to remove it (a ring keeps three). Each change is the ROI at once (its statistics read again) and a step of Undo (Ctrl+Z); Shift+R, Esc or Enter end the editing. A rectangle edited becomes a polygon of four vertices. Not a GIS editor: one ROI, its vertices only
Save ROI as vectorView → Save ROI as vector... (or the command palette): the ROI (a rectangle or a polygon, holes kept) as a GeoPackage (.gpkg), GeoJSON (.geojson) or shapefile (.shp, its text in UTF-8), by the name's extension, in the active layer's CRS (a GeoJSON in WGS 84 when the CRS has no EPSG code, as RFC 7946 asks), a feature with name, layer and pixels; Open it as a vector layer adds it to the map. Alt + click it later makes the same ROI again, the same pixels inside. A project (File → Save project) keeps the ROI too
Vector layersFile → Add vector layer..., the Layers panel (Add vector layer...), a drop or the command line: GeoJSON, Shapefile, GeoPackage (each of its layers), KML, FlatGeobuf, GML, GPX or a CSV of points; listed in the Layers panel with the series (a new one on top): show/hide, colour, labels (a column's values on the map), move, remove; right click → Zoom to it, Attribute table, Extract series, Interpret. Hovering a point shows its attributes (lines and polygons: hold Alt); see Vector layers
Series at points or polygonsa vector layer → Extract series...: the active layer or every visible one, a row per feature (a column per date) or a row per feature and date; CSV
Interpretation (labelling)a vector layer → Interpret... (the Interpretation panel): N / Shift+N (or Page Down / Page Up) next / previous feature, 1–9 its label, 0 clears it, D the date of the change (the date on the map), Shift+D none; notes; Export table...
AnimationFile → Export animation (Ctrl+Shift+A): dates (from, to, step), frame rate, resolution, GIF / MP4 / WebM, date stamp, legend, scale bar, pins, ROI and vector layers; see Animation
Time←/→ previous/next date, P play/pause, click or drag on the chart; the time bar above the map (play, the date slider, the speed) shows with a series of two dates or more, not with a single image or vector layers alone. Under the slider, each date's availability: a bar as tall as the share of the visible area that is valid on that date (no cloud, no gap; of the overview), red under half; the pointer over it gives the share, a click goes to the date
Map mode, colormap, rangeDisplay panel, for the active layer (range is automatic 2–98%, or typed, or dragged on the histogram)
HistogramDisplay panel, under the range: the values shown (0.5–99.5% of them) filled in the colours the map gives them, dimmed outside the range, the colormap strip under it; drag a triangle (or its line) to move an end of the range, between them to move both, double click for the automatic range again; the pointer over it shows a bar's values and share. Click a bar to highlight its pixels on the map, the others dimmed to grey (click it again: none); Shift + click adds bars, Shift + drag a range of values; its share of the pixels under the histogram, Clear to end it. With Largest drop: date, a bar is a date: what dropped then. --mode NAME,highlight=LO:HI from the command line
Change between datesDisplay panel → Difference (value - reference): pick the Reference (a date, or Previous date (t-1)); diverging colours centered at 0, follows the time bar
Temporal compositeDisplay panel → Temporal composite: median, mean, maximum, minimum or number of observations of each pixel over a window: the shown date's year (the arrows and playback then go year by year), some days around the date (a moving window) or the whole series; with the season, only its dates. Computed in the map shader over the overview's dates each time the map is drawn (the median of up to 64 values: every k-th one beyond)
When it greensDisplay panel → Seasonal peak (when it greens) (dated series, 6 dates or more round the year): each pixel's annual harmonic (v = m + a cos θ + b sin θ, θ the date's time of year) fitted by least squares to its dates with a value (in the season), as a colour: the hue the time of year it peaks (a wheel of the months on the map and in the panel, the cursor's peak marked), the saturation how much it rises and falls (the stretch: the peak-to-peak amplitude, 0 to its 98th percentile), the brightness its mean (Brightness by the mean, from a quarter; off: all bright). A September soybean and an April second crop in different hues, an evergreen forest or water grey; dates all in a few months give no fit (not drawn). The status bar gives the cursor's peak date, amplitude and mean; the PNG export a legend of the months. Computed in the map shader over the overview's dates
SeasonDisplay panel → Season → Only part of the year: a window of days of the year (presets by months: DJF, JJA, Apr–Sep...; a start after the end wraps over the new year and belongs to the year it ends in). The dates outside it are left out of the temporal statistics (mean, trend, std...), the composites, playback and the arrow keys; the chart shades the season. Applies to every layer with dates
Largest dropDisplay panel → Largest drop: date or magnitude: the largest decrease between consecutive valid observations (no-data dates skipped), dated at the lower one; the colour bar shows dates. Exact values for the cursor and pins in the Statistics panel
Classes (categorical data)Display panel → Categorical (classes): legend with colours, names and shares (click a colour to change it, untick a class to hide it); detection can be switched off or forced. Classes over time... (under the legend, and on the chart's toolbar) opens View → Analysis → Classes: Shares (each class's share at every date, its legend beside the chart: a click on a swatch hides or shows the class; one date, or a stack's band: a bar per class), Transitions (the matrix of two dates as a heatmap, the largest changes beside it) and Flows (Sankey). On the chart, a categorical layer's series has styles of its own: Steps + markers (the markers in the classes' colours), Steps, Markers or Class blocks (a block per date in its class's colour); every class is named on the Y axis. Values, trend and Y = map range do not apply to class codes and are disabled
Band, index, cloud maskDisplay panel → Bands (one file per date with several bands): band A, optional normalized difference with B, quality band; Apply reopens the layer in place
Spectral index, expressionDisplay panel → Index or expression: an index of the Awesome Spectral Indices (275, searched by name or domain; only those the series has the bands for: roles N, R, RE1, S1... placed by wavelength or band name, constants and wavelengths in place), or an expression typed over the bands (2.5 * (N - R) / (N + 6*R - 7.5*B + 1), nd(nir, swir1), B08 > 0.3 = 1); Apply reopens the layer showing it: map, charts, ROI, Zeit's tools, exports and Copy Python follow it. --expr EVI (or a text) opens the inputs so. Open in calculator takes it to the raster calculator
Raster calculatorTools → Raster calculator...: an expression over the open layers, each by a short name in the Layers list (s2.nir, dem, "any layer".band4); bare band names are the active layer's. A series with an image uses the image at every date; two series are matched by date (the same day, the nearest within N days, the same month or year: a date without a match is no data); a layer on another grid is resampled, in another CRS reprojected (Options: whose dates, whose grid, the resampling, the quality masks). Operators + - * / % ^ < <= > >= == != and or not, name = expression lines, rules condition = value (the result starts from the condition's first operand, or result = ...; x == nan tests no data), functions (where, coalesce, clamp, nd, bit, qa, math...), the date's year, month, doy... One argument of max, min, mean, sum, median, std (the population's, numpy's), count, percentile reduces a series over time to an image (no data skipped; ndvi - mean(ndvi) is each date's anomaly); at(ndvi, 2003) is one of its dates (a year, 200307 a month, 20030715 a day; the Layers list gives each date's), at(ndvi, 2020) - at(ndvi, 1990) two of them. Over time, in the series' real dates: argmax(ndvi)/argmin the date (decimal year) of the largest/smallest value, first(ndvi < 0.3 and year >= 2020)/last(...) of the first/last date a condition held, longest(ndvi < 0.3) the longest it held in days, persist(ndvi < 0.3, 3) 1 where the last 3 observations held; slices of the calendar median(ndvi[2019-06 .. 2019-09]), mean(ndvi[11 .. 2]) (those months of every year); periods max(ndvi) by year, mean(ndvi) by month (a series of the years or months); windows mean(ndvi, 90d) (the dates of the 90 days up to each, w weeks, y years); lags ndvi[-1], lag(ndvi, 2) (the pixel's previous observations with a value), lag(ndvi, 1y) (the nearest date a year before); anomaly(ndvi, base=2015..2019, by=month) (each date's z-score against its month in the base years; by=doy, window=15d). Live shows the result on the map as it is typed (the overview's size, a layer marked preview; a reduction drawn as its dates are read, "max so far: 23 of 107 dates"; a series at the date shown); Chart gives its values at the cursor or the first pin under the editor (the result's series, or an image's value with the values its reductions reduce; a part of the text selected drawn too). A reduction read by several dates (ndvi - mean(ndvi), an anomaly's climatology, (s - min(s)) / (max(s) - min(s))) is computed once, on every thread, into an image beside the result, by a virtual layer too (each date computed it again); a result's overview reads only the rows it shows, as a series' own does, also through a lag's or a window's VRTs (41 dates of 7318 × 7329, 8 threads: s - mean(s) 7 s + 5 s, s * 2 2 s, mean(s, 3y) 6 s, s - s[-1] 23 s). Janus reads the result's VRTs itself: their files straight, each file's block by one thread, on the processing threads (eight at most), the values GDAL's VRT gives bit for bit (GDAL reads what it does not cover: a file on the network, another kind of VRT); on the guide's 107 dates of Sentinel-2, 3 threads, count(nd(N, R) > 0.5) is on the map in 0.8 s (2.6 s through GDAL's VRT), a pin's 107 values in 0.1 s (1.1 s), its median written as a COG in 1.1 s (3.7 s). A band of one file with overviews, zoomed out, shows the expression (GDAL's VRT showed the file's overview: x * 2 as x). While a result's dates are computed, a bar on the map and one in the calculator say so (Computing "calc": 12 of 41 dates). The editor colours the text, completes names (Tab/Enter, Ctrl+Space), explains the name under the pointer and underlines an error as it is typed; Ctrl+Enter or Run adds the result as a layer: VRTs computed as the map reads them, or cloud-optimized GeoTIFFs (a task). History and favourites kept; Examples; the index library inserts formulas. --calc TEXT [--calc-run]
Regularize seriesTools → Data preparation → Regularize series...: the active series at a fixed step (8 or 16 days, monthly, yearly, any number of days; periods from the first date's day, month or year, as pandas' resample, the empty ones too): each period's median (each band's), medoid (the observation nearest the bands' medians, so its bands come from one date; zeit.regularize_time_series) or clearest date (the value of the period's date with the most clear pixels that has one); the band, index or expression shown with its quality mask, or every band (masked). Empty periods left empty, or filled linearly in time or from a Whittaker curve (λ; the values kept, the ends not extended) when the values around are at most N days apart. On the whole layer or the ROI, in blocks of rows on the processing threads; a COG per regular date (<name>_<YYYYMMDD>.tif) in a folder that opens as a new series when done (a task in Tools → Tasks; its provenance kept)
Speckle filterTools → Data preparation → Speckle filter...: a radar series (Sentinel-1's VV and VH) through Quegan's multitemporal filter (each date's window mean times the mean, over the dates with a value, of each date's value over its own window mean; Quegan & Yu 2001: the speckle averaged through time, each date's changes kept) or Lee's (each date alone: the window's mean plus the pixel's departure from it, weighted by how much more the window varies than the speckle of L looks does; Lee 1980; Sentinel-1 IW GRDH 4.4 looks); a window of 3 to 15 pixels, cut by the series' edges, counting the pixels with a value only. Every band of every date on the linear values (not dB), the whole layer or the ROI, in blocks of rows on the processing threads; a COG per date in a folder that opens as a new series shown as the one filtered (its dB)
Harmonize sensorsTools → Data preparation → Harmonize sensors... (zeit's bandpass_adjust): a series that mixes Landsat and Sentinel-2 has a step wherever the sensor changes, which CCDC or BFAST read as a break. The Sentinel-2 dates go through the bandpass adjustment of HLS (Claverie et al. 2018; HLS v2.0 User Guide, table 5): a line per band and unit (2A, 2B, 2C; unknown taken as 2A), OLI = slope × MSI + intercept, for the coastal, blue, green, red, narrow NIR (B8A) and SWIR bands; Landsat 8 and 9 stay as they are (OLI is the reference, as in HLS). Landsat 7 and 4-5 stay as they are too unless asked: then Roy et al. 2016's lines (reduced major axis or least squares), fitted on pre-collection data. Each date's sensor comes from its scene (the STAC item a search's VRT records, else the file's name: S2B_MSIL2A_..., LC08_L2SP_...) or is chosen for all; HLS products are refused (already adjusted). Sentinel-2's broad NIR (B08) has no line and is left as it is (search with B8A to adjust it). The values are reflectance or reflectance × 10000, as found (the intercepts scaled). Join with another open series on the same grid (a Sentinel-2 search and a Landsat one, the second reprojected onto the first's grid): both adjusted, their dates in one series, the bands they share named by role (Blue, Green, Red, NIR (narrow), SWIR 1, SWIR 2), in the units of the first, each masked by its own quality band. Only HLS's bandpass step, not its atmospheric correction or BRDF normalization. The whole layer or the ROI; a COG per date in a folder that opens as a new series; --window harmonize[-run]
PolygonizePolygonize... in the menu of a run's map or of a series (its date shown) in the Layers panel: the map's patches (pixels of one value, 4 or 8 neighbours) as polygons in a GeoPackage that opens as a vector layer, each with its value, class (the class names), date (a map of years), area_ha and perimeter_m (geodesic, on the CRS's ellipsoid), pixels and the mean of another map of the same grid (mean_<map>, a loss's magnitude). A minimum area first merges the smaller patches into the neighbour they share the longest border with (the minimum mapping unit of Post-process), a patch with none is left out; the outlines can be simplified (a tolerance in metres, their topology kept). A task in Tools → Tasks; its provenance kept
RasterizeRasterize on the series' grid... in a vector layer's menu: its features burned on the active series' grid (its CRS, origin, pixel size and size; the features reprojected to it) through GDAL's own rasterizer (the same pixels as gdal_rasterize): 1 inside, 0 outside (a mask), the feature's number (1, 2... in reading order) or an attribute (a number as it is; a text as classes, numbered by name, their names and colours on the layer); the pixels whose centre is inside or every pixel touched; a later feature over an earlier one. A task whose GeoTIFF opens as a layer, ready as a Zeit tool's mask (Only where ... is not 0, under its scope); its provenance kept
Zonal statistics over timeZonal statistics over time... in a vector layer's menu: each feature is a zone (its pixels those whose centre is inside, or every pixel touched; a pixel in several features counts in each), through every date of the active series or a run's map, on every feature or within the ROI: for values each date's count, mean, standard deviation, least, percentiles 10, 25, 50, 75, 90 and largest; for classes each class's pixels and area (each pixel's true area, as in Areas) at every date and the transitions between two dates; for a map of change dates the area by year. The zones named by an attribute or their FID. A task writing zonal_long.csv (a row per feature and date, and class), zonal_wide.csv (a row per feature, a column per date: the statistic chosen, or each class's ha), transitions.csv, and a GeoPackage of the features with those columns added, opened as a layer; Analysis → Zonal draws a feature's series; its provenance kept
Reproject, resample, clipTools → Data preparation → Reproject, resample, clip...: the active series' files (or a run's map) through gdalwarp's own code (the same result as the gdalwarp command, whose arguments the window and the task's log show): to a CRS (EPSG:4326, ESRI:102033, a PROJ string, a WKT), the CRS of a layer or the grid of a layer (its CRS, origin, pixel size and extent: the maps aligned pixel to pixel), a pixel size (optionally aligned, -tap), resampling near, bilinear, cubic, average, mode (the default for classes), min, max or med; the whole layer, the visible area, the ROI or the polygons of a vector layer (the pixels outside them without a value, cropped to them); no data, data type; COG, GeoTIFF or virtual (warped VRTs: nothing written, ready at once). File by file on the processing threads, into a folder that opens as a new series (a task; its provenance kept)
RGB of three bandsDisplay panel → RGB composite (one file per date with several bands): Three bands of each date as RGB, a preset (true colour, colour infrared, SWIR, agriculture, land/water: bands found by their names or wavelengths) or any three bands, the map's date or a fixed one, the stretch of each channel (2–98% of the first image, kept for every date; Stretch to this image). The chart, the cursor and the tools keep the series' band or index; zoomed in, the visible area is read again at full resolution; map panels, the swipe, PNGs and animations show it too
Python of a seriesTime series panel → Python... → a pin or the ROI: code (numpy, rasterio) that reads the same series from the files (band, normalized difference, quality mask; the ROI's pixels inside it), prints its statistics and, with a Zeit tool on the chart, makes the same Zeit calls with the same parameters (as the tool made them: recorded, not rewritten); shown in the Python history's editor, to read, change, copy or save
Python historyTools → Python history... (or the palette): every finished run as Python, kept between sessions (history.jsonl in Janus' settings folder, the last 5000). See Python history
Reset layoutView → Reset layout (Ctrl+Shift+R, Mac: Command+Shift+R): every panel docked where it was at the first start, the floating windows (Exports, Tasks, Log, Settings) back to their first size and place, map panels to the right of the main map; the panels open stay open
Performance panelView → Performance (hidden by default, and not kept open from one session to the next): timings, threads in use, Zeit status, overview memory, full-resolution cache (progress, size, read times, Build it now), disk cache (what the caches take, their budget, the disk's free space)
SettingsFile → Settings... (Ctrl+,, Mac: Command+,): the interface (Modern or Classic) and its theme, font size, whether the Files panel follows what is opened, processing threads, overview memory, the disk cache budget (automatic or set by hand), full-resolution cache (when it is built) and clearing the caches; kept between sessions (see Settings)
Several seriesLayers panel (+ Add) or File → Open (Ctrl+O): each opens as a new layer; several images that are not dates of one series: File → Open files as separate layers... or a drop with Shift. The panel is a table of contents: the active layer's opacity on top, then one list, top of the list drawn on top, the basemap its last row (under every layer); Add embeddings folds under it: series, the maps of the runs and vector layers in one order, as in a GIS (a new series or map goes over the other rasters but under the vector layers, a new vector layer on top; a vector layer can then be moved under a raster one, or a raster over it); a row a layer (the eye shows or hides it, a picture of it in its colormap or geometry, its name over its dates or kind, the date shown at its right, a ⋯ menu while the pointer is over it); click a series to make it active (Space shows or hides it), double click to zoom to it, drag any row onto another to reorder. Right click (or ...): make active, zoom to it, opacity, move (to the top, up, down, to the bottom), Export (map as PNG, values or rendered view as GeoTIFF, animation), close; a vector layer's: colour, attribute table, interpret, extract series, zoom to it, Export as GeoPackage, GeoJSON, Shapefile or CSV, remove. The arrow unfolds a series: its dates (a stack's bands, unfolded from the start) a row each, the one shown with its eye open (a click or its eye shows another; its menu exports that date alone or opens it as a layer of its own). The maps a run makes (LandTrendr's year of detection, magnitude...) are layers of their own, not rows of the series: each its eye, its place in the order, its group; hiding or closing the series leaves them on the map. A map's arrow unfolds its colormap and range, or its classes' legend; a click selects it (the Display panel then shows its colours, and Pixel values its histogram); its menu: opacity, Show only this map, move, group, Save as GeoTIFF, save every output of its run, remove (Delete removes the ones selected; the files stay on disk). With five or more, a filter by name keeps the list short
Blend, styles, groupsLayers panel: the active layer's blend mode beside its opacity (Normal, Multiply darkens by the layers under it, Screen lightens, Add sums, Darken and Lighten keep the darker or lighter of each channel), also under Blend in a series' menu (--blend MODE on the command line). A row's menu → Style: Copy style (its mode, each mode's colormap and the ranges set by hand, the stretch per date, the RGB bands, opacity, blend, its classes' names, colours and visibility; a vector layer's colour), Paste style on the layers selected (or the row), the saved styles (kept in the settings, given with a click, x deletes one) and Save style under a name. Groups: select rows (Ctrl/Shift + click) → Group the N selected: they go next to each other in the drawing order under a row of their own, whose eye shows or hides them all, whose arrow folds them, whose click selects them (Delete closes them) and whose menu renames it, moves it to the top or the bottom, ungroups it or closes its layers; a row dropped on a member (or on the group's row) joins it, Out of its group takes one out. The palette has Blend: ..., Copy style of the active layer, Paste style on the selected layers and Group the selected layers
BasemapLayers panel → Basemap (the list's last row): its eye shows or hides it; click the row (or its arrow) to pick a source (None = nothing downloaded); opacity in its ⋯ menu; S shows or hides satellite imagery (Esri World Imagery, or the imagery source picked); Custom XYZ URL: the URL ({z}, {x}, {y}; {-y} for TMS rows; applied when you leave the field), the attribution to show, the finest zoom and the tile size. The source and its settings are kept between sessions, but it starts hidden, as does every series opened (its eye shows it); the map panels' and the swipe's layer list has Basemap only
Web layersFile → Add web layer... (also + Add in the Layers panel and the palette): a server's URL or a preset (TerraBrasilis' DETER and PRODES, IBGE, an OGC API demo); the service found from the URL (OGC API - Features, WFS, WMS tried in turn) or chosen (WMS, WMTS, WFS, OGC API - Features); Connect lists its layers (title, name, the abstract on hover; a filter by name, title or abstract). A map (WMS, WMTS): Add map layer puts it on top of the drawing order, drawn as the basemap (Web Mercator tiles around the view, a GetMap per tile through GDAL's WMS driver; WMTS by a Google-compatible tile matrix set, its image formats only: vector tiles are not drawn; a dimension such as Time at the server's default), with its style, format, Transparent, opacity and, for a layer with a time dimension, the server's default, a time typed, the series' date (the last time listed not after the date shown) or up to the series' date (from the first time to it); its credit on the map and in the exports; its row's menu: opacity, time, reload its tiles, move, remove; Map info: a click on the map asks the visible WMS maps whose layer is queryable what is there (GetFeatureInfo at their time, in GeoJSON, plain text or HTML, whichever the server offers first in that order; the tolerance in pixels as drawn), the window listing each map's features and fields. Features (WFS, OGC API): the visible area, the ROI, the active layer or the whole layer (the box sent to the server), At most (50000 by default), a date field with two dates and an attribute filter (OGR SQL; both sent to the server when it takes them); Fetch features is a task of Tools → Tasks (progress, Cancel): paged into a GeoPackage in the cache's web folder (the same request within 12 h read from it; files older than 7 days removed), opened as a vector layer named after the server's layer ((first N) and a notice when the cap was reached); every vector tool works on it, Export as... keeps it. A WFS's fields and features are read with the capabilities the window already has (GDAL's driver does not ask for them again: 1.4 s instead of 3.7 s on IBGE). Errors (no connection, the server's error, a bad URL) are said in the window; nothing waits on the interface. Projects keep the maps and the fetched layers' requests (fetched again when the GeoPackage is gone). --web-layer URL,LAYER[,SERVICE][,KEY=VALUE...] adds one once the series is open (keys time=DATE|series|upto, field=, from=, to=, max=, opacity=, area=0..3, dialog=1, filter=). Compared with geopandas, OWSLib and requests: tools/bench_ogc_vs_python.py, bench/ogc-vs-python.json
Official alertsValidation & uncertainty → Official alerts... (the Validation panel's Alerts tab): a run's map of change dates (LandTrendr, CCDC, BFAST, CODED...) against official alerts (or a map of dates from disk: a layer or a file, in decimal years, YYYYDDD, YYYYMMDD or days since 1970, detected), on the map's grid, over the area both cover and a window of dates: DETER (INPE; TerraBrasilis' WFS, Amazon or Cerrado, fetched for the map's area in a task and opened as a vector layer), any vector layer of dated polygons (a date field, a class field), or alert rasters: UMD's GLAD-L and GLAD-S2 (read from UMD's public GeoTIFFs for the map's area, no key, or from files), Wageningen's RADD and GFW's integrated alerts (their GeoTIFFs need a GFW API key: open them from disk, or Of the map's area reads GFW's public map tiles, zoom 14, and decodes their colours). Compare (a task of Tools → Tasks) gives the area of change in both, only in the map, only in the alerts; the alerts the map detects (by area, by count, by their own area) and the map's change the alerts confirm (by area, by patches), Dice; the lag (the map's date minus the alert's: median, quantiles, the share within 30, 90 and 365 days, a histogram); by class (DETER's classname) or confidence; the agreement map (both, only the map, only the alerts) and, for rasters, the alerts' dates join the layers; Export CSV... writes the summary, the classes, every alert, the lags and the agreement map. See Official alerts. --alerts SOURCE[,KEY=VALUE...] compares once a map of change is there (mapfile=PATH, dates=auto|decimal|yearday|ymd|days for a map from disk)
Browse filesFiles panel: double click opens, right click → Add as layer or Add to favorites; Ctrl+click selects several files; hover a folder for what it would open as. Opening a series expands the tree down to it (Settings → Files panel follows what is opened)
Add by droppingdrop files or a folder on the window: a new layer (several files make one series of their dates; with Shift held, each file a layer of its own)
Seasonal views, classes over time, scatterView → Analysis (see above)
Chart of several layersTime series panel → All visible layers (one marker shape per layer)
Second monitordrag a panel's tab out of the main window
Maps side by sideView → New map view (Ctrl+T): pick the layer and, if wanted, its own date and mode in the panel's bar; every panel follows the same pan/zoom; close it with its tab's x or Ctrl+W (the focused panel, else the last one opened)
SwipeView → Swipe (C): drag the divider (white line with a handle); the bar above the map picks what is right of it: a layer and, if wanted, its own date and mode, or Basemap only; Swipe off or C again closes it
Space-time transectCtrl + drag a line on the map (Mac: Command + drag), or T / View → Draw transect, then drag; a polyline (a river, a road, a valley): T, then click its vertices, a double click or Enter ends it (Backspace undoes a vertex); Alt + click a line of a vector layer: the transect along it; Esc cancels. Transect panel: distance from A along the line (X; dashed verticals at the bends; no data where a polyline leaves the layer) × dates (Y, oldest on top); hover a cell = distance, date, value, marked on the map; click = go to that date; Values / Anomaly (− each place's mean); Copy CSV (a row per date, a column per sample); Clear, or close the panel
Profiles of every lineProfiles of every line... in a line layer's menu (Layers panel): every line (each part of a multi-line) sampled about a pixel apart along its length, as the transect samples it, through every date of the active series or those from one to another; the values the chart shows. A task (Tools → Tasks: progress, cancel; the processing threads) writing profiles.csv, a row per sample and date (fid, the fields chosen, part, sample, distance_m (metres; distance_map_units in a CRS without an EPSG code), x, y, col, row, date, value; samples off the series left out), and optionally profiles_wide.csv (a row per sample, a column per date) and the samples as points, profiles_points.gpkg or profiles_points.shp (the wide table's rows in the series' CRS: fid_line, the fields, part, sample, the distance, col, row and a column per date; a shapefile's names cut to 10 characters, at most 255 columns); its provenance kept
Chart optionsstyle (lines ... bars; a categorical layer: steps, markers, class blocks), values/anomaly/z-score/seasonal anomaly/CUSUM, trend (OLS/Sen), Y = map range, stripes, the ROI's spread (p10–p90, box plot, fan, density)
Map as a figureFile → Export map as PNG... (Ctrl+E): resolution (1×, 2×, 4×), background, date label, legend, scale bar, pins, ROI and vector layers; Save to: the file (a path, a name alone for the last export folder, or Browse...), then Export (or Enter)
Data for QGISFile → Export values as GeoTIFF... (Ctrl+Shift+E; the active layer at the date: visible area or whole image) or Export rendered view as GeoTIFF... (Ctrl+Shift+V; RGBA as shown, georeferenced)
ProjectsFile → New project / Open project... / Save project (Ctrl+S) / Save project as... / Recent projects: a .janus file (JSON) keeps the series (their files, band, index or expression, quality mask, date, style, opacity, blend, visibility), the vector layers (colour, visibility), the runs' maps (their GeoTIFFs, colours, range), the drawing order, the groups, the active layer, the pins, the ROI (box or polygon), the transect, the view, the swipe, the map panels, the basemap, the web layers (the maps, and the fetched layers' requests), the saved views and the season. Paths are kept relative to the project's file (and absolute, used when the relative one is not found), so a folder with the project and its data can be moved or shared; a file not found leaves its layer out with a notice, the rest opens. The window's title gives the project's name, * when it has changes not saved; New and Open ask what to do with them (Save, Discard, Cancel); closing Janus does not ask, the session (changes included) is kept. Opening a .janus file (File → Open, a drop on the window or jn work.janus) opens the project. The session is kept every minute and at exit (last-session.janus beside Janus' other data) and, with Settings → Reopen the last session at start turned on (off by default), reopened at the next start
UndoCtrl+Z undoes the last change to the layers, Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y redoes it; Edit → Undo / Redo says what (Undo Opacity of NDVI, Undo Close Landsat). Undone: closing layers (a series, a vector layer, a run's map: opened again in their place, with their style and date), opening them, styles, opacity and blend, colours, the drawing order, groups, visibility, names, pins, the ROI and the transect. A slider or a layer dragged is one step, whatever the frames in between; panning and zooming, the date shown, the panels and the active layer are not steps. The last 100 steps are kept; opening a project or New project starts again. A text field keeps its own Ctrl+Z
Save a tool resultright click it in the Layers panel → Save as GeoTIFF..., or File → Export Zeit result as GeoTIFF. A copy of the result: Float32, full resolution, the series' grid and CRS, no data = NaN, named <layer>_<tool>_<output>.tif
Save every output of a runright click a result → Save all outputs of this run... (Ctrl+Shift+S for the run of the result on top): all of them (e.g. LandTrendr's year of detection, magnitude, duration, rate, DSNR, values before and after) into a folder at once; the popup lists the files and warns before replacing one
Save embeddingsFile → Export embeddings as GeoTIFF... (Ctrl+Shift+M; when a layer is drawn as embeddings): the view shown, visible area or whole layer, at full resolution; see Embeddings
Export progressFile → Exports (Ctrl+J; opens by itself with each export): progress, cancel, open the folder
Shortcuts on a MacCommand instead of Ctrl (e.g. Command+E, Command+Shift+S)
Series as textCopy CSV in the Time series and Transect panels
Zeit toolsTools menu, grouped by the question asked in the order of a workflow (Data preparation: Tmask, Smoothing, Interpolate, Standardize, clear-sky observations, ImproPhe, Regularize, Speckle filter, Harmonize sensors, Reproject; Spectral analysis: NDFI, spectral unmixing; Temporal dynamics: phenology, Mann-Kendall, AR(1) trend, temporal metrics, fold by period, linear trend of a fold, polar phenology; Change detection: CAT (change, aftereffect, trend) and the others; Spatial pattern analysis: emerging hot spots, SNIC, texture; Classification & pattern recognition: TWDTW, SOM, k-means, post-processing, the Classification window, field delineation; then the raster calculator and Tasks) → tool window (parameters, chart fitting, raster runs); progress in Tools → Tasks
Zeit logsTools → Log (or Log next to a task): the log of each raster run, followed live (what ran, its progress, outputs, the end or the error); Copy, open the file or its folder
Tool resultslayers of their own in the Layers panel (over the rasters): show/hide, order, groups, colormap, range, opacity, a class map's class names (edited in its legend); their values at the cursor and pins, histogram and statistics in Pixel values (in the chart's place while a map is shown over its series)
EmbeddingsView → Embeddings: principal components as RGB (of every year, or local to the ROI), similarity to the cursor, a pin or the ROI, change between years; see Embeddings
Add embeddings of the visible areaLayers panel → Embeddings (above the basemap): AlphaEarth or TESSERA, years, cell size, visible area or ROI, then Add embeddings; progress on the map, the layer comes on top when it is ready

Clicking a legend entry hides/shows that series together with its trend line. Hovering the chart shows the date under the pointer: a dashed line, each series' value marked on it, and a card with the values (the ROI's p10 and p90 under its mean; the class's name for a categorical layer). The main series (the cursor's, else the ROI's mean, else the last pin's) has an area fading under it; trend lines are dashed; with Lines + markers the markers are left out when the dates are closer than 7 points.

Zeit tools

The Tools menu lists the algorithms of Zeit that Janus exposes (step-by-step guides with screenshots on the website: LandTrendr, CCDC, CODED and the NDFI, BFAST, Phenology, the AR(1) trend and the Trend test):

ToolSeriesMaps
LandTrendrannual (one date per year)year of detection, magnitude, duration, pre/post value, rate, DSNR of the chosen loss/gain event
Mann-Kendallany (seasonal variant: several dates per year)significant Sen's slope, slope, p-value, Z, tau, trend class, intercept
Emerging hot spotsany, ≥ 3 dates (raster runs)the pattern (no pattern, 8 kinds of hot spot, 8 of cold spot, named and coloured), the Gi* of every date as a new layer (hidden: show it, or hover it for a pixel's Gi* series), the trend of the Gi* (z), the dates a hot / cold spot
AR(1) trendany (harmonics: several dates per year)significant slope, slope (per year or per time step), p-value, t, its standard error, AR(1) rho, intercept, residual SD
BFASTregular, ≥ 2 dates per yeartrend/season break counts, date and magnitude of the largest trend break
BFAST Literegular, ≥ 2 dates per yearbreak count, date and magnitude of the largest break, first break date
BFAST Monitorregular, ≥ 2 dates per yearfirst break date in the monitoring period, magnitude, break yes/no
Phenology≥ 6 dates per yearstart, peak and end of season (day of year), length, peak value, amplitude, fit R², seasons — for a typical year (median), the latest season or a chosen year
CCDCone file per date with blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2 [+ thermal]; a quality band is recommendedbreak count, largest break date and magnitude, NDVI change, first/last break, segments
CCDC synthetic imageas CCDCthe image CCDC's models predict for a date (Date, a decimal year; 0 = the date on the map): every band in the series' units and the quantity shown (e.g. NDVI), without clouds or gaps
CODED (degradation)one file per date with blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2, ≥ 2 dates per year; a quality band is recommendedstrata (forest, non-forest, degradation, deforestation, disturbance), first and last change dates, NDFI change, changes, mean NDFI of the training period
NDFI (spectral unmixing)one file per date with blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2the NDFI of every date as a new layer (and, if asked, the GV, NPV, soil and shade fractions), mean and lowest NDFI, observations used
Tmask (cloud screening)one file per date with green and SWIR1, ≥ 2 dates per yearobservations flagged and their share; the series shown without them as a new layer
TWDTW classificationdatesclass map (one class per pattern, with a legend), distance, margin to the 2nd class
Post-processing (classes)a categorical layer (one map or a map per date)the classes cleaned as a new layer with the layer's names and colours: each pixel's short excursions removed (A B A becomes A A A), then each date's map through a majority filter and a minimum mapping unit that merges the small patches into the neighbouring class; how many dates of each pixel changed
SOM clusteringanycluster map (the typical series of the cluster under the cursor is drawn on the chart; with samples, each cluster named by them), distance to it
k-means clusteringanycluster map, ordered by the centres' mean value (the centre of the cluster under the cursor is drawn on the chart; with samples, each cluster named by them), distance to it
SNIC segmentationanysegments (a colour each), each segment's mean series as a new layer, the segments' polygons (GeoPackage, opened as a vector layer) with their size, centre and mean of every value compared
Texture (GLCM)any (raster runs only)a map per feature of a temporal summary of the shown series in a moving window: the GLCM's contrast, dissimilarity, homogeneity, ASM, energy, correlation, entropy, mean and variance, and the window's mean, standard deviation and Sobel gradient
Agreement of change mapsmaps of dates from other tools (any series)consensus year, how many maps agree (and their share), maps with a change, spread of the years
Interpolate (regular grid)dates (a series with real dates)the series on a regular grid of dates (FORCE's TSA interpolation, as zeit.interpolate: from the first date, every Step days, 16 by default) as a new layer with one band, and one date, per grid date; radial basis functions (an ensemble of kernels, Kernel widths), linear, moving average (Window) or a robust harmonic fit (Harmonics, Trend); dates with nothing within reach are empty
Temporal metrics (FORCE STM)anya map per chosen metric of each pixel's whole series (FORCE's STM, as zeit.temporal_metrics): minimum, 5th/10th/25th/median/75th/90th/95th percentile, maximum, range, interquartile range, mean, standard deviation (n - 1), skewness, excess kurtosis, number of observations
Fold by period (FORCE)dates (a series with real dates)the same metrics by Period (year, quarter, month, week or day of the year; the calendar has 365 days, 29 February sharing day 60 with 1 March), one new layer per metric with a band per period: by year it opens as a yearly series, the others as stacks of named bands (Q1, Jan, week 01, doy 001)
Linear trend of a fold (FORCE)dates (a series with real dates)FORCE's trend analysis, as zeit.linear_trend of zeit.temporal_metrics by period: one Statistic (mean by default) is folded by Period (year by default), a least-squares line is fit over the periods (x = the period's position, so the slope is per year when folded by year; periods without a value count as steps but are skipped), and a map is written per chosen statistic of the fit (slope, offset, gains, R², significance of the slope at Confidence level with a two-sided or one-sided test, errors, periods with a value); a pixel run draws the yearly values and the line
