Change, aftereffect, trend (FORCE CAT)dates (a series with real dates)FORCE's CAT, as zeit.cat of the same fold: the greatest loss between a period with a value and the previous one (optionally weighed by its recovery, CHANGE_PENALTY), when it happened (the year, or the period's number), and the linear trend of the whole fold, before the change and after it, one map per chosen statistic; a pixel run draws the yearly values, the lines before and after and the change
Clear-sky observations (FORCE CSO)dates (a series with real dates)FORCE's clear-sky observations, as zeit.clear_observations: windows of Window months from the first day of the first date's month (the last window kept whole), and for each chosen statistic a new layer with a band per window, labelled with its first month (2020-03, so it opens as a monthly series): the number of valid observations (not missing after the quality masking) and statistics of the gaps in days between them (shortest, longest, mean, quantiles...), the window's edges counting as ends of gaps; a pixel run lists the windows
Polar phenology (FORCE)dates, a regular series (a constant step of whole days over at least 2 years: run Interpolate first and use its result)FORCE's polar land surface phenology, as zeit.polar_metrics (Brooks et al. 2020): the 39 metrics of each year's season (dates of its start, middle, end, peak and minima, values, amplitudes, lengths, integrals, rates of rise and fall), one new layer per metric with a band per calendar year; the date metrics (D*) are days since 1 January of the band's year; the thresholds of the season's start, middle and end (0.2, 0.5, 0.8) and the adaptive start are parameters; a pixel run lists the metrics by year and marks the dates on the chart
Standardize (FORCE)anythe series minus its mean, or also over its standard deviation (z-score), as a new layer on the run's dates (zeit.standardize)
Tasseled Cap (FORCE)any (real dates; bands blue, green, red, nir, swir1, swir2)FORCE's Tasseled Cap, as zeit.tasseled_cap: brightness, greenness, wetness and FORCE's disturbance (brightness - greenness - wetness of the same matrix, not Healey's index) of each date, in reflectance x 10000; a raster run writes one series per component and opens each as a new layer. Coefficients: Crist 1985 for every sensor (FORCE's, the default), each date's sensor (TM Crist, ETM+ Huang 2002, OLI Baig 2014, MSI Crist; see below) or Huang 2002 or Baig 2014 for all dates; Reflectance units automatic by default
Spectral adjustment to Sentinel-2A (FORCE)any (real dates; bands blue, green, red, nir, swir1, swir2)Landsat 4-9 or MODIS reflectance on the spectral response of Sentinel-2A (Scheffler et al. 2020, as zeit.spectral_adjust): all ten bands, red edge 1-3, broad NIR (B8) and NIR (B8A) included, one series per band opened as new layers. Sensor: each date's own (default; see below) or one fixed for all dates (LND04..LND09, MOD01 Terra, MOD02 Aqua); FORCE's first cluster search reproduces FORCE's integers exactly. Sentinel-2 dates are refused
NBAR (c-factor)any (real dates; at least one of coastal, blue, green, red, rededge1-3, nir, nir08, swir1, swir2, and bands sza, saa, vza, vaa unless the angles come from Sentinel-2's metadata)nadir BRDF-adjusted reflectance (Roy et al. 2016, 2017, as zeit.nbar): each mapped band times the c-factor of the MODIS Ross-Thick / Li-Sparse-Reciprocal model, taking the date's sun and view angles to nadir view and a normalized solar zenith; one series per band (and per c-factor with Also write the c-factors) opened as new layers, in the input's units. Normalized solar zenith: each date's scene mean (default) or a fixed angle; Sun and view angles from: four bands of each date or Sentinel-2 granule metadata; Angle bands' unit: degrees or hundredths of a degree (see below)
ImproPhe (FORCE)any (real dates; every band of each date, the quality band applied) and another open series in the same CRS to sharpensharpens a coarse series to the pixels of this finer one, as zeit.improphe (FORCE's CF- and L2-ImproPhe; Frantz et al. 2016): each pixel takes the weighted mean of the coarse values of the pixels of its neighbourhood that look like it in the fine data. Raster runs only; a band for each layer (and band) of the coarse series, on the grid and window of this series, opened as a new layer with the coarse series' dates. Coarse series, The coarse series is (a field with a layer a year, or scenes), Seasonal windows, Kernel radius and Texture radius (in map units), Variance kept, FORCE's arithmetic, Components; see below
Smoothinganychart only: the smoothed series (Whittaker or Savitzky-Golay)

Mapping the bands of Tasseled Cap and the spectral adjustment. Both need the six reflective bands mapped to blue, green, red, nir, swir1 and swir2. For Sentinel-2, map B8A to NIR (FORCE's choice, not B8); for MODIS, map SWIR1 and SWIR2 to bands 6 and 7.

The sensor of each date (needed by Each date's sensor in Tasseled Cap and by the spectral adjustment's default) is read from the scene the date came from: the STAC platform or item its VRT records, else its file name (LC08_..., LT05_..., S2B_..., MOD09...), in FORCE's names (LND04..LND09, MOD01, MOD02, SEN2). A date whose sensor is not found is an error that names the dates (the same for a Sentinel-2 date in the spectral adjustment). In that case choose a fixed matrix (Crist 1985, Huang 2002 or Baig 2014 in Tasseled Cap) or a fixed Sensor (spectral adjustment), which do not read it. Copy Python gives the Zeit call with bands= mapping the six roles to the layer's bands (Zeit looks for swir16 and swir22 where Janus calls them swir1 and swir2) and sensor= with the sensors found; only the observations the quality band keeps are passed.

Mapping the bands of NBAR. The tool reads the four angle bands of each date, mapped to the roles sza, saa, vza and vaa (solar zenith and azimuth, view zenith and azimuth), which are bands of the same series as the reflectance: Landsat Collection 2's SZA, SAA, VZA and VAA bands (the Level-1 angle bands) or angle rasters stacked with the bands of each date. Map also every band to normalize (any of coastal, blue, green, red, rededge1, rededge2, rededge3, nir (Sentinel-2's B08), nir08 (B8A, OLI's band 5), swir1, swir2; at least one, or the run stops saying so). Set Angle bands' unit to hundredths of a degree for Landsat Collection 2 and HLS (they store 3025 for 30.25 degrees); angles from Sentinel-2's tile metadata are in degrees. Hundredths read as degrees give a map of missing values, but degrees read as hundredths give a wrong result without a warning. Each date's scene mean of the solar zenith is taken over the pixels of the run's window whose four angles are valid (the angles are read once over the whole window before the maps are computed), so it changes with the window; on the chart there is no scene, and each date is brought to nadir at the pixel's own sun. A pixel with a zenith outside 0-90 degrees or an angle without a value is missing. The bands must be reflectance (the factor is a ratio, so any scale will do, but not Landsat Collection 2 digital numbers with their offset); the quality band is not applied. HLS is already NBAR. Copy Python gives zeit.nbar with the angles as a Dataset (scaled by the unit) and bands= mapping the roles.

NBAR of Sentinel-2 from the tiles' metadata. Sentinel-2 L2A files carry no angle bands, but every tile's MTD_TL.xml has the sun's and the view angles on a 5 km grid. Set Sun and view angles from to Sentinel-2 granule metadata (MTD_TL.xml) and the angle roles need no band (map only the bands to normalize): the angles of every pixel are computed as Zeit's zeit.sentinel2_angles does, the view angles of the detectors of one band fused cell by cell (Sentinel-2 view band, B06 as HLS does, for every band) and everything interpolated bilinearly to the pixels (Roy et al. 2017), and Angle bands' unit is not used (they are in degrees). Where a date's metadata is found: in a series made from STAC items (Earth Search's granule_metadata asset, Planetary Computer's granule-metadata) the date's VRT records the items' hrefs (STAC_GRANULE_METADATA; Planetary Computer's are read with the same token as its bands); for local files, in the product the file is in (X.SAFE/GRANULE/<granule>/MTD_TL.xml) or an MTD_TL.xml beside the file. A date without metadata stops the run, naming it; so does a metadata of another date (sensed more than a day from it). A date of several tiles takes the angles of the first one that has a view angle at the pixel. Pixels outside the tile's grid, or that no detector sees, are missing. Copy Python then gives zeit.sentinel2_angles(sources, like=nbar_cube, view_band=...) (the hrefs or paths, one per date; Zeit signs Planetary Computer's if planetary_computer is installed) on the cube placed on the files' grid, before zeit.nbar.

ImproPhe: picking the coarse series, and its two modes. The series in the window (the active layer) is the fine one, whose pixels the output takes; the series to sharpen is another open layer, picked in Coarse series (a menu of the other open series with their dates and bands; one in another CRS is listed but cannot be picked: reproject it first, Tools > Data preparation > Reproject). The coarse series may be on any grid of the same CRS: each fine pixel takes the coarse pixel its centre falls in (nearest neighbour, as FORCE's read does), and where the coarse series has no pixel or no value the output is empty. Each band of a coarse date is a field of its own (the phenology metrics of a year, the bands of a Landsat scene) and is sharpened with the same neighbours; a quality band of the coarse series is not one of them, and a coarse series shown through an expression gives its files' bands. The fine series gives every band of each date but its quality band, which masks the dates it refuses (NaN) before the fine scenes are averaged in the seasonal windows. The coarse series is: a field with a layer a year (CF-ImproPhe: a 500 m phenology metric of each year; the years of its dates must differ) is sharpened year by year with the fine scenes of that year (a year with no fine scene keeps its coarse values), and the scenes of a sensor (L2-ImproPhe: Landsat at 30 m for Sentinel-2 at 10 m) are each sharpened with the seasonal means of all the fine dates. Detected takes several dates in a year for scenes, and asks about a series with one date a year. The output has a band for each layer (and band) of the coarse series, named by its dates. The radii are in the map's units and become pixels of this series by truncation (2500 m and 330 m are 250 and 33 pixels of 10 m, FORCE's defaults): the cost of a pixel grows with the area of the circle, so try 300 to 500 on the preview or a small ROI first. The window is held whole in memory (the components are of the whole window): a window needing more than 6 GB is refused with the memory it needs, and the whole layer is too large for most series: choose the ROI or the visible area. The estimate in the window is analytic (pixels, dates, bands, layers and the circle's area, fitted on runs of three radii). Over the MCP the fine series is series and the coarse one coarse of run_tool. Copy Python reads both series (the fine one over the window, the coarse one whole) into cubes and calls zeit.improphe(coarse_cube, fine_cube, by=..., ...), checked to give the run's values.

TWDTW classes come from the series itself: drop pins on places you know (forest, crop, pasture...) and give them a class in Tools > Classification & pattern recognition (the window opens on TWDTW): each class's mean series of its samples is its pattern, and the method is estimated on the samples by place. The distance is that of the R package twdtw: a pattern may match any stretch of the series, and dates without a value are left out of each pixel's series. By default time is measured between the dates (Time measured), so patterns should cover the same period as the series, and dates more than a year apart are never matched (Max time apart); measured between days of the year, a pattern of one season matches that season in any year.

CODED (Bullock et al. 2020) monitors forests with the NDFI of every observation: a model of the NDFI over a training period (by default the first 3 years; Monitoring start moves it), then Consecutive observations more than Threshold RMSEs below it are a change. After a change, the land is forest again (degradation: selective logging, understory fire) when the new model's mean NDFI is at least Forest NDFI (0.5), otherwise deforestation. On the chart: vertical lines at the changes, and, when the layer shows a normalized difference, the NDFI of each observation and the training mean. The NDFI tool gives the index itself (Souza et al. 2005: near 1 in closed forest, below 0 on soil and pasture) as a series of the same dates, a new layer on which LandTrendr, BFAST or the agreement can run.

Tmask (Zhu & Woodcock 2014) flags the observations whose green is too bright (cloud) or whose SWIR is too dark (shadow) for a robust harmonic model of the pixel's own series: haze and thin clouds a quality band misses. The flagged dates are marked on the chart; a raster run writes the series shown without them as a new layer. The model spans the whole series, so after a sudden lasting change (a clearing) observations may be flagged too: look at such pixels on the chart.

SOM clustering trains a Self-Organizing Map on a sample of the area (rows spread over it, Training sample pixels) and gives every pixel the nearest neuron: pixels with alike trajectories share a cluster, and neighbouring clusters are alike. Each pixel needs a value on every date: gaps are filled linearly in time (or the pixel is left out). Hover the cluster map: the chart draws the typical series of the cluster under the cursor, in its colour.

k-means clustering (Janus' own, as scikit-learn's KMeans: k-means++ starts, Lloyd's iterations, the best of Starts runs) fits its centres on the same sample of the area as the SOM, its gaps filled the same way, and gives every pixel the nearest centre; the clusters are ordered by their centres' mean value, low to high. Against scikit-learn 1.9 on the same series (8 kinds of NDVI-like trajectory, 60 dates, 8 clusters, 10 starts): the same partition (adjusted Rand index 1.0 on 20 000 pixels, 0.99996 on 200 000) and inertia (within 4e-8), 1.2 times as fast on one thread and 1.5 times on four (tools/bench_kmeans_vs_sklearn.py, bench/kmeans-vs-sklearn.json).

Run from the Classification window with samples (its Samples tab), the SOM and k-means name their clusters by the samples in them: each cluster takes the class of most of its samples, each place (a polygon, a pin) counting once however many pixels it has, as in Forest (cluster 3, 21%); Forest or Pasture (cluster 2, 9%) when no class has two thirds of them; Cluster 4, 6%, no samples when none falls in it. The samples are read as the run reads the area, so a sample is in the cluster its pixel has on the map.

SNIC segmentation (Achanta & Süsstrunk 2017, as zeit.snic and R's sits_segment) divides the area into segments of neighbouring pixels whose whole series are alike: every date of the shown band or index (or, with Values compared: Every band, every band of every date) is one value compared. Segments grow from seeds every Seed spacing pixels on one of R snic's grids; Compactness trades regular shapes for following the data, and is in the values' units (0.5 for reflectance or an index in 0-1, thousands for reflectance x 10000). The area is segmented in tiles (Tile size) on every core, and segments never cross a tile's edge. Gaps are filled in time as for the SOM. The run writes the labels (snic_labels.tif, Int32, -1 outside every segment), each segment's mean series (snic_mean.tif, opened as a layer: the series as objects) and the polygons (snic_polygons.gpkg, layer segments: supercells, x, y, n_pixels and a column per value compared, named date or date_band), opened as a vector layer for interpretation by object.

Texture (GLCM) (as zeit.texture) maps the texture of the shown series: first a summary of its dates (Summary of the dates: median, mean, minimum, maximum, standard deviation or amplitude, the 95th minus the 5th percentile), then, in a Window of 7 pixels about each pixel, the grey-level co-occurrence matrix's properties (Haralick et al. 1973) as scikit-image's graycomatrix(symmetric=True, normed=True) and graycoprops give them, averaged over four directions at the Pair distance, the values quantized to Grey levels over the summary's 2nd to 98th percentile; and three of spfeas's window statistics (the mean, the standard deviation and the mean Sobel gradient). Fields, pastures, orchards, plantations and forests differ in texture where their spectra are alike: the maps are predictors for the Random Forest (Beside the series) and show the grain of a landscape. The windows need their neighbours, so it runs on the raster only. Zeit's texture equals scikit-image's to 1e-12, 78 times faster on one thread.

The agreement runs on maps Janus already shows, not on the series: check two or more results whose values are dates (LandTrendr's year of detection; CCDC, BFAST or CODED dates), from any layer. A date counts by its calendar year, and maps agree when their years are at most Tolerance apart; the consensus year is the one most maps agree with. The outputs are on the grid of the first map checked (the others are put on it), as layers of their own.

A break's date (BFAST, BFAST Lite, BFAST Monitor) is that of the first observation after it, and its magnitude the model after the break minus the model before it on that date, as in Zeit's extract_events.

On the chart, the BFAST family draws its fitted model with the breaks: BFAST, the piecewise linear trend (a segment between trend breaks) plus the harmonic season (its own between season breaks), and the trend alone, lighter; BFAST Lite, trend + season refitted between its breaks; BFAST Monitor, the history's model and, lighter, where it goes over the monitoring period (what the observations are compared with). Zeit returns the breaks, not the models: Janus fits them again by least squares, on Zeit's regular time axis.

The CCDC synthetic image follows the map: with Date 0 its chart marker (the predicted value, on the CCDC segments) moves with the date shown, and a raster run predicts the map's date (named in the task's title).

"Regular" means evenly spaced dates (monthly, 16-day...): a missing date must be a no-data band, not a skipped one. BFAST and BFAST Lite are slow (~2–3 ms per pixel on all cores): use the visible area or an ROI before a whole scene.

Multiband tools show a Bands section in their window: which band of each date plays each role (guessed from the band names, e.g. NIR, SWIR1; unnamed stacks of 6+ bands are taken as Blue, Green, Red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2). CCDC, CODED, the NDFI and Tmask work on reflectance × 10000 internally; reflectance 0–1 and Landsat C2 Level-2 digital numbers are detected and converted (parameter Units, decided once per run). CCDC's model is drawn in the units of what the layer shows (a band or a normalized difference).

Each tool window has:

  • Parameters, generated from the tool description sent by Zeit (hover a field for help). Tools that do not fit the open series are disabled with the reason (e.g. LandTrendr needs an annual series).
  • On the chart: on as soon as the tool is opened (closing its window takes it off): fits the model to the cursor, pin and ROI series and draws it over them (LandTrendr segments and vertices, Sen's line, vertical lines at break dates); the model's numbers are added to the Statistics table. Several tools can be fitted at once (e.g. LandTrendr, Mann-Kendall and the AR(1) trend, or phenology and smoothing): each in its own colour and line (solid, dashed, dotted), named in the chart's legend (a click there hides that tool's models; hiding a series hides its models), the same line shown next to the checkbox and over the tool's rows in the Statistics table; changing one tool's parameters fits only that tool again. On a series that does not suit the tool (e.g. LandTrendr on a monthly series) the checkbox is off and disabled, with the reason; it fits again on a series that does. With All visible layers on the chart, single-band tools are also fitted to the other layers' cursor and pin series. Python... gives the calls of every tool fitted on the series.
  • Estimated run time for the chosen scope, measured by Zeit on samples of the series (a fixed cost per block plus a cost per pixel, and the fit of tools that learn from a sample, such as the SOM; reading the data is not included).
  • Run on the raster: whole image, visible area or ROI; Only everywhere or where X is not 0, X a layer on the series' grid (a vector layer rasterized, a class map): its pixels 0 or without a value are left out and have no value in the outputs. The run happens in the background on the processing threads of Settings (every logical core but 2 by default), with progress and cancel in Tools → Tasks. Outputs are GeoTIFFs (default folder %LOCALAPPDATA%\Janus\results) loaded over the map as layers of their own in the Layers panel (the first output shown, the others hidden); cells without an event are transparent. Series outputs (the NDFI, a screened series) are one file with a band per date, added as a layer over the others (the active layer stays).
  • Preview (under Run): the tool on the ROI, or without one on at most 256 x 256 px at the centre of the view, in a folder of the work folder; its maps open as layers marked preview (the badge in the Layers panel), its window dashed on the map (Preview... while it runs), and the next preview replaces them (their folder deleted). Auto-preview previews again a moment after a parameter changes, when a preview is estimated to take 3 s or less; the window warns when the parameters changed since the preview shown. Closing the tool's window removes its preview; Run then runs on the whole scope as before.
  • A log of every raster run, job.log in the run's results folder (next to job.json and the outputs): the tool, its parameters, window and threads, the progress (every 10% or 5 s), each output, and how it ended (with the error, if any). Tools → Log shows it while it grows (pick the run in the list), as does the Log button of each task.
  • Provenance of every result, provenance.json in the run's folder (Zeit tools, deep learning models applied, the raster calculator): the tool, the versions of Janus and Zeit (zeit-core's revision), when it ran and for how long, how it ended, the series it read (its files, the band, index or expression shown, the quality mask), the scope and the window in pixels, the parameters (those not at the tool's default named), what else it took (the model's file and post-processing, the calculator's text and layers) and the files it wrote. A result's menu in the Layers panel (a run's map, or a series a run or the calculator wrote) gives Provenance... (all of it in a window, the changed parameters in the accent colour), Run again with these parameters... (the tool's window with them and the same scope; on the same series, the scope The run's window is the very window it ran on, even if the ROI has moved since), Python of the run... (the run's code in the Python history's editor: a Zeit tool's rerun.py reads the series over the run's window from its files, makes the same Zeit calls with the same parameters and writes every map they return as a GeoTIFF, numpy, rasterio, xarray and zeit-cdts; Reproject, resample, clip, Rasterize, Polygonize, Zonal statistics, Regularize, Build series and the calculator's simple expressions have a rerun.py too, see Python history) and Open folder.

Python history

Tools → Python history... lists every processing run that finished, newest first, as Python: a Zeit tool's run, the calculator's results, Reproject, resample, clip, Rasterize, Polygonize, Zonal statistics, Regularize and the other tools that keep a provenance. Opening, viewing and closing layers do not count, nor runs cancelled or failed. The history is kept between sessions (history.jsonl in Janus' settings folder, the last 5000 runs), and an entry stays when its run's folder is deleted.

Each entry's code starts with what ran (Janus' version, the tool, when, the series and scope, the run's folder and files). Then it has one of two kinds of code:

  • A script (rerun.py, also written beside the run): a Zeit tool's run reads the series over the run's window and makes the same Zeit calls with the same parameters. The other tools' scripts are short because they are written with Zeit (zeit.load_raster and zeit.save_raster read, warp and write the files), and carry only the branches their run took. Reproject, resample, clip is load_raster(file, crs=, res=, resampling=) and save_raster for each file (outside the footprint Zeit writes no data where gdalwarp writes 0); only what Zeit cannot do (pixels aligned to the size, a no data value or type of the output, a cutline, an extent together with another CRS) stays gdal.Warp with gdalwarp's options. Rasterize burns the same features with the same values on the same grid through rasterio's rasterize and save_raster. Polygonize traces the same polygons with rasterio.features.shapes (the same simplification, the minimum area through Zeit's mmu_sieve) and measures their geodesic areas and perimeters with pyproj, into a GeoPackage of the same columns. Zonal statistics burns each feature alone and writes the same long and wide tables (and the transitions), pixel areas as Janus measures them. Regularize is Zeit's regularize_time_series over the series read by load_raster (median or medoid; the clearest date by a few lines of xarray), its gaps filled (linear, Whittaker through zeit.smooth). Build series calls gdal.BuildVRT (and gdal.Translate for COGs) with the same grid, as Zeit writes no VRT. The calculator's expressions without reductions over time or stages, on layers of the same grid, read the inputs with load_raster as Janus' VRTs read them and compute the expression in numpy, date by date, written by save_raster. Each script writes its files in a python folder of the run, and the UI self-test checks that they equal Janus' own (rasters value for value, GeoPackages feature for feature, tables cell for cell; the calculator within 1e-5, as Janus computes in float32).
  • The run as data (as data in the list), for the tools that have no script yet: the parameters, inputs, window and outputs as Python values, with the equivalent command when there is one.

The editor beside the list colours the code and can be edited: Copy, Save .py..., Save notebook... (a Jupyter notebook), Revert (back to the run's code), Open folder, Provenance and Remove (the entry only). All as .py... and All as notebook... write the entries shown (the filter on top searches tools, folders and code) as one script with a # %% cell per run, or one notebook; Clear history... empties it. The chart's and the validation's Python... buttons show their code in the same editor, without adding it to the history.

How it works: Zeit's methods are compiled into Janus: zeit-core (the Rust core of Zeit) with what Zeit's Python adds around it (bands by role, the NDFI's unmixing, the BFAST family's refits...), giving the same numbers as Zeit's Python API (the tests compare them tool by tool). A fit of the chart's series takes under a millisecond, so models follow the cursor; a raster run reads the series in bands of rows (from the full-resolution cache when it has the dates) and computes them on every processing thread. Nothing starts at startup and no Python runs.

Time series analysis (FORCE)

Tools → Time series analysis (FORCE)... is FORCE's TSA as a chain rather than a list of tools. It runs the eight tools of the Tools menu that make it, with the parameters their own windows hold (change a parameter in either place, the other sees it), in this order:

  1. Clear-sky observations, on the raw series (its quality band is read here);
  2. Interpolate, on the raw series: the analysis series, on a regular grid of dates;
  3. Standardize, on the analysis series;
  4. Temporal metrics, Fold by period, Linear trend of a fold, Change, aftereffect, trend and Polar phenology, each on the analysis series.

The default is Interpolate, Temporal metrics and Fold; a step is a checkbox. The steps after Interpolate or Standardize read the series they write (their GeoTIFF, opened again as a series), so the chain gives what FORCE's TSA gives, and the numbers are those of the tools run one after the other. A step the series cannot take (Polar phenology needs a regular series) is left out and said so.

The window has three tabs:

  • Input: the series the chain runs on (the active layer): how many dates, from and to, whether they are regular or irregular (Interpolate puts irregular dates on a regular grid), the band shown and the quality band, or that there is none.
  • Steps: the eight steps with their parameters (the same fields as the tool's window), the reason when the series cannot take one, the pixel chart and To look at.
  • Output: the scope (the whole image, the visible area or the ROI), the output folder, Run, Copy Python, the task's progress and, once it is done, Use in Classification.

To look at reads the dates and the parameters of the steps that are on, before anything runs: a year inside the series with few dates, a first or last year only partly covered (for the steps that read years), an Interpolate grid denser or much coarser than the dates, a missing quality band (Clear-sky observations counts every date as clear), a trend over fewer than five years, a step the series cannot take and a chain with nothing on. Each is a coloured dot (information, something to look at, something that stops a step); the Steps tab shows how many need a look.

The pixel chart (Steps tab) follows the pixel last hovered on the map and runs the chain on it: the observations (grey, and in the series' colour where the quality band keeps them), the analysis series as a line on Interpolate's grid, and the overlays of the steps that have them (the trend's line, the fold's values, the polar phenology's dates), each in its own colour under the step's name; the steps that gave no chart or failed are listed under it. Temporal metrics and Clear-sky observations give rows only, no overlay. It is computed off the interface's thread, and again when a parameter changes.

Run is one task (Tools → Tasks), in a folder of its own, <series>_tsa_<time>, with a subfolder per step (01_interpolate, 02_temporal_metrics, 03_fold...): each has its job.json, job.log, provenance.json and rerun.py and its outputs, as the tool's own run has. The folder itself has the chain's provenance.json (the steps with their parameters and folders, the series, the scope, the versions, how it ended; its result layers open it with Provenance..., and Run again with these parameters... turns the same steps and scope on in this window), rerun.py and job.log. The maps (Temporal metrics, Linear trend, CAT) arrive as result layers and the series (Interpolate, Standardize, Fold, Polar phenology, Clear-sky observations) as layers, all named by their step (Temporal metrics: Mean); the active layer does not change.

Copy Python copies one script that does in Zeit what the chain does on this series and scope, even before it runs: the series read once from its files, each step's call (those of the tools' own scripts; the steps after Interpolate and Standardize read the variable analysis) and every result written as a GeoTIFF. It is the same script the run keeps as the folder's rerun.py.

Use in Classification (a menu of the series the chain wrote: the interpolated, the standardized, the metrics by period, the phenology by year) makes the one chosen the active layer and opens the Classification window: it reads the dates of the active series as its features, so the samples are classified on the chain's series instead of the observations.

--window tsa opens the window on the Steps tab (the defaults on the whole image); --window tsa-run also runs the chain.

Classification (Random Forest, TWDTW, embeddings, SOM, k-means, networks)

Tools > Classification & pattern recognition > Classification trains a model on samples you already have in Janus and classifies every pixel by its whole series, without Python: a Random Forest (Breiman 2001; the first in the list: quick, on the CPU, good with few samples), TempCNN (Pelletier et al. 2019: convolutions over time) or L-TAE (Garnot & Landrieu 2020: attention over the dates), the networks as the authors built them (written from their papers and reference code, with their training settings), trained and applied on the GPU (the same wgpu as the map; the CPU without one).

  • Samples from the interpretation's labels, a validation project's references (the adjudicated label, else the interpreters' when they agree), a vector layer's class column (points, or polygons: their centre, each pixel inside up to a number, or the mean of their pixels; SNIC's segments are such polygons), or pins given a class in the window (the source the window opens on). The classes keep the label set's order.
  • Pins by class (source Pins): a list of classes (type a name, Add; its colour, its count of pins; x removes it), the class new pins get (a click on the map drops a pin of it: drop a class's pins one after the other), the pins without a class given one at once; Coloured by class gives each pin its class's colour, the one the class map will show. A new class takes the first colour no other class has, from a palette of colours each as unlike those before it as can be (Tableau 10's, then Glasbey's farthest in CIELAB); a click on a class's colour picks another. The project and undo keep each pin's class and each class's colour.

  • One window for every classifier, the method chosen in it (tab Method), on the same samples and their quality check:

    • learned from the samples: the Random Forest and the networks below;
    • matched to each class's series: TWDTW (Zeit's): each class's mean series of its samples is its pattern (no pin to pick per class: every sample counts), with its settings (time weight, time measured, max distance); Classify the cursor, pins and ROI on the chart gives each series its class as it is fitted; Apply runs it on the raster (whole image, visible area or ROI, its preview);
    • on a layer of embeddings: the Embeddings panel's logistic regression or nearest centroid, fitted on the samples' vectors in the year shown; Apply makes the samples the layer's classes and shows its Classes view;
    • without samples: the Self-Organizing Map (Zeit's) and k-means, run from Apply; with samples, each cluster is named by the class of most of the samples in it (Names of the clusters in the Method tab, the last run's clusters below it). Tools > Classification & pattern recognition > TWDTW, SOM and k-means open this window on them. TWDTW and the embeddings' classifier are estimated on the samples as the forest is, cross-validated by place (5 folds; at most 3000 samples classified): the estimated accuracy, kappa, the confusion matrix (with the samples left unclassified) and each class's accuracy, the forest's check beside it, so the methods are compared on the same samples (s2ro, 54 pins of three classes: TWDTW 91 %, the forest 96 %).
  • The window has three tabs: Samples (where they come from and their quality), Method (the method, the values, its settings, its training or estimate) and Apply. It opens as wide as half the screen and lays the Samples tab in two columns when there is room, in one when narrow; every list scrolls in a box of its own, so the window never grows past the screen.

  • The samples' quality, as they are gathered: whenever the samples change (a pin dropped or moved to a class, a polygon labelled), after a short pause and in the background, Janus reads the new places' series (each pixel once) and grows quick forests cross-validated by place (each sample classified by forests that never saw its place, 5 folds, 60 trees each). It shows:

    • a summary: the samples, the classes, the estimated accuracy (with a small curve of it as the samples grew), the warnings, and the verdict on the last pin dropped ("looks like Pasture, 92 %", or "looks more like Soy: check it");
    • the classes: samples and places, their balance, each class's accuracy and the class it is most often taken for (a click shows its samples);
    • what to look at, the worst first: samples that look like another class (mislabelled, or a mixed place: their pins ringed in red on the map), samples of different classes on the same pixel, classes of few samples or few places, unbalanced classes, classes taken for one another, samples left out for too few dates with a value (a click shows those samples), and bunched samples: with 10 places or more, the forests are cross-validated again on kNNDM folds (as far from the training as the map is from the samples); an accuracy 5 points below the place-by-place one or more ("somewhat bunched"; 10 points: "bunched") says that the samples cover the area unevenly and the map far from them will do worse: samples from the places left out help. The summary shows it as the accuracy far from the samples;
    • each class's typical series: its mean and p10-p90 band on each date (of the value chosen), where the classes part and where they overlap;
    • the samples' table: each pin or place with its class (a pin's changed there), how well it fits its class (its class's probability, or the class it looks like), its share of dates with a value, > to go to it and x to remove a pin; filtered (all, those that look like another class, on a shared pixel, without a class, a class) and sorted (in order, least fitting first, by class). Only the rows seen are drawn: thousands of samples scroll smoothly. The estimate guides the gathering; the training's validation is the measure. --window classification opens it on the pins; --pin X,Y,CLASS drops a pin of a class.
  • Values read on each date: the series shown (the band or normalized difference, the quality band applied) and, with several bands per date, any of the source bands (screened by the quality band too). Gaps are filled linearly in time; pixels with values on fewer than Min dates with a value are left out. Each value is scaled by its 2-98 % quantiles of the samples (sits' normalization).
  • Training (a task in Tools > Tasks, cancellable): a validation share split off each class or, for TempCNN, by place (seeded; 20 %), Adam at 1e-3 (TempCNN: batches of 32, up to 150 epochs, patience 20, no decay of the rate; L-TAE: batches of 128, 100 epochs), the classes optionally weighed, early stopping on the validation loss (Patience); the model of the best validation loss is kept. With few samples the batch is made smaller, so that an epoch has at least 8 batches (with fewer, the batch normalizations' statistics are too rough and the model classifies everything alike). The window draws the loss and accuracy curves and, at the end, the validation samples' confusion matrix with the user's and producer's accuracies.
  • Random Forest: Trees (500), the values tried at each split (auto: the square root of their number, a date's values each a value), the samples in a leaf at least (1) and the depth at most (no limit), as R's randomForest and ranger and scikit-learn's defaults: each tree grown on a bootstrap sample, each split the best by the Gini impurity among the values drawn, a pixel's probabilities the mean of its leaves' class shares over the trees. The validation share is held out by whole places (all of a polygon's pixels on one side), so the accuracy is that of places the forest never saw; the out-of-bag accuracy (each sample by the trees that did not see it) is drawn beside it as the trees grow. At the end, the importance of each date (the mean decrease of the impurity, summing to 1; by value too, with several): the dates that tell the classes apart. With Importance: by permutation too, also the out-of-bag accuracy lost when a value is shuffled (each tree's out-of-bag samples classified again, ranger's importance = "permutation", unscaled), which does not favour values of many levels; the trees take about twice as long. The trees grow on the CPU's threads, each from its own seed: the same forest whatever the threads. Against scikit-learn and R's randomForest on the same samples (tools/bench_forest.py, 500 trees each), the same test accuracy within a point (the mean of 3 seeds: 0.904, 0.907 and 0.903 on sits' MODIS NDVI samples; 0.865, 0.875 and 0.875 on its Landsat-8 of Rondonia, where one of the 32 test samples is 3 points; 0.827, 0.826 and 0.825 on 20,000 made-up samples of 64 values); grown 3.5 times faster than scikit-learn and 2.5 times faster than randomForest on one thread (19 s, 66 s and 47 s on the 20,000 samples), 5.4 s on four threads (scikit-learn 16.7 s); the test samples classified as fast as they are on one thread, 1.4 times faster on four. Against ranger 0.18 too: the same accuracy within a point, grown 2.8 times faster on one thread (56 s) and 2.3 on four (14 s); with the importance by permutation, 39 s on one thread against ranger's 93 s and randomForest's 126 s, the same ten most important values as randomForest's and nine of ranger's (Spearman 0.90 and 0.85 over the 64, the uninformative ones near 0 in any order; 0.95 to 0.99 on sits' samples).

  • Validation (the settings of the forest and the networks): how the places are held out, so that the accuracy is not that of places next to those the model learned from (blockCV, Valavi et al. 2019; CAST's kNNDM, Linnenbrink et al. 2024; as Zeit's spatial_folds). Each place (a polygon, a pin) is a point, its pixels' middle, in metres.

    • kNNDM (the default, recommended): see below. If its folds cannot be made (too few places, no coordinates), the training says so and holds out whole places at random instead.
    • Whole places at random: the validation share of each class's places.
    • Spatial blocks: a grid of hexagons or squares, the blocks dealt into Folds at random (the most even of 100 draws, each fold near a k-th of each class's places), in rows, or as a checkerboard (squares, 2 folds). Their size is given, or found from the values read: the median range of the spatial autocorrelation of up to 12 dates' values, semivariograms of 2000 pixels drawn at random, each the spherical, exponential or Gaussian model that fits best (blockCV's cv_spatial_autocor, zeit-core's variogram).
    • Buffer around the places tested: the validation share of the places, and the places within the distance of them out of the training too (blockCV's cv_buffer).
    • Clusters (k-means): the places' mean values, standardised, in k clusters (blockCV's cv_cluster): a validation of conditions the model has not seen; or, measured on the map, their positions (a fold's places together).
    • kNNDM: the places grouped by Ward's hierarchical clustering (k-means beyond 4000 places, or chosen) into q clusters, merged into k folds of about equal size, for q from k to the number of places; kept, the folds whose distances from each place to the nearest place of another fold are distributed most like those from the map (a grid of about 1000 cells) to the nearest place. The window draws the three distributions, as CAST's plot of knndm. Measured between the values (CAST's and Zeit's space="feature"): the distances between the places' series (each date's bands, standardised by the places'), and from the series of about 1000 pixels of the area to the most alike place: a validation of values the model has not seen, wherever they are.

    With folds, the forest is cross-validated: a forest for each fold, grown on the others, predicts its samples (the confusion matrix is of every sample), and the forest kept is grown on all of them. A network is cross-validated too (Cross-validate, on by default; k+1 trainings): a network for each fold, trained on the others and stopping early on places of its own training, predicts its fold, and the confusion matrix is of every sample; the network kept validates, and stops early, on one fold (the one whose classes the others keep best), its accuracy there shown beside. Off, the network is only trained on that split. The area of applicability takes the folds as CAST does (each sample's dissimilarity to the samples of the other folds), and its error profile the cross-validation's predictions. Show the folds on the map makes them now and opens them as a vector layer coloured by fold (the blocks and the places; written as a GeoPackage in the results folder's folds); a training writes its folds beside the model (<model>.folds.gpkg). Spatial folds choose a model and calibrate its area of applicability; a map's accuracy is still estimated from a probability sample (Validation & uncertainty; Wadoux et al. 2021). Against Zeit's spatial_folds on the same points (crates/janus-ml/tests/folds_zeit.rs): the same blocks in rows and as a checkerboard, the same buffers, Ward's clusters as scipy's, k-means as tight as scikit-learn's, and kNNDM's folds as near the map's distances (W 130.4 against 129.7, from different random draws) in 0.03 s against 0.07 s (k-means: 1.0 s against 3.2 s), for 1000 places.

  • What this means (the Model tab, after a training, or a model opened): the validation read in plain words, the most pressing first: how good the accuracy is (good from 85 %, fair from 70 %) and how it was measured (as far from the training as the map, on places at random, or on pixels of the places learned from); with fewer than 100 validation samples, the range the accuracy could be in (95 %); each class found less than 70 % of the time and the class it is taken for, with what to do (samples of both, from more places, where they differ; or join them); a network that learned its samples by heart (15 points more on them than on the others); a forest whose out-of-bag accuracy is far above its spatial one (neighbouring samples alike); kNNDM suggested when the validation was not spatial; and that the map's own accuracy comes from a probability sample.
  • Beside the series (the forest's settings): rasters on the series' grid read as further predictors, one value each a sample after its series' values: the maps of runs on the series (Texture (GLCM)'s above all, see below) and single rasters open of its size (a DEM, a distance map). A raster may cover part of the series (a run's ROI) but must have its pixel size and be aligned with it; pixels without a value in one are left out. A polygon's mean takes their mean too. The model keeps their files' paths and reads them again when it is applied; their importance is listed after the dates'.
  • The model is kept in a .janusmodel file (in the results folder's models): its weights and what applying it needs (the architecture, the values and dates, the scaling, the classes and their colours, the samples and the training's history). Open a model... applies one to another series of the same number of dates and the same values (bands by name); the window says what does not fit.
  • Apply to the whole image, the visible area or the ROI: the class map (Byte, with the classes' colours and names in the file), the probability of the class given and the uncertainty (the entropy over that of equal probabilities: 0 sure, 1 undecided) open as result layers, ready for the validation (the uncertainty as a stratum, too). Before applying, the class map can be post-processed as Zeit does it: Smooth the probabilities (Bayesian smoothing, Camara et al. 2024, written from the paper; it agrees with bayesEO to about 2e-3: each class's probability pulled towards its neighbours', the more where they agree; window, smoothness and neighbours as in the paper) and a Minimum mapping unit (patches of fewer pixels merged into the neighbouring class of the longest border); the uncertainty stays the model's. For a map you already have, Tools > Classification & pattern recognition > Post-processing (classes).

  • Area of applicability (Meyer & Pebesma 2021, as Zeit's aoa and R's CAST): where the model can be trusted. A Random Forest, TempCNN or L-TAE model keeps its samples' series as it reads them (gaps filled, scaled; up to about a million values, as many of each class as their share) and the threshold of their dissimilarity: each sample's distance to the nearest sample of another place (another polygon or pin), over the mean distance between samples, and the threshold the upper whisker of those (75 % quantile + 1.5 IQR). Applied with Area of applicability ticked, it also gives the dissimilarity index of each pixel (its distance to the nearest sample over that mean) and the AOA (Byte: 1 inside, 0 outside, 255 not classified): outside it the class is an extrapolation the validation says nothing of. The tick's tooltip gives the model's samples and threshold; older models, Presto's and U-TAE's keep no samples. A forest's values are weighed by their importance (as CAST weighs a model's variables): a date that does not tell the classes apart does not make a pixel unlike the samples.

    • Error profile (CAST's errorProfiles, Zeit's error_profile): the validation samples (whole places held out from the training) sorted by their DI to the samples of the other places, the accuracy in moving windows of 5 of them, and a curve that only falls fitted to those (a monotone P-spline). The model keeps it; the Apply tab draws it, and an applied model gives the expected accuracy of each pixel inside the AOA (NaN outside), a continuous map of its uncertainty.
    • Local point density (ticked under Area of applicability; slower): how many training samples are as near a pixel as the threshold, i.e. whether the model learned from many samples like it or from one.
    • Mahalanobis distance (Classification window, Settings: Area of applicability by the Mahalanobis distance; CAST's method = "MD"): the samples whitened by their covariance, so values that move together count once. It needs values of full rank: a series' filled gaps are combinations of the dates around them, and then the Euclidean distance is kept (the task's log says why).
    • Validation & uncertainty > Area of applicability (AOA)... opens the Apply tab with Only the area of applicability ticked: the DI, the AOA, the LPD and the expected accuracy, mapped without classifying (the network is not run).

Presto (Tseng et al. 2023) is pretrained by its authors on monthly series of Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, ERA5 and SRTM worldwide. Janus runs its encoder with their weights (3 MB, downloaded once from their repository and checked against their SHA-256; without network, put default_model.pt in a folder and set JANUS_WEIGHTS to it): the series' bands are matched to Presto's inputs by name (blue, green, red, rededge1-3, nir, nir08 or B8A, swir1, swir2, VV, VH, elevation, slope, or the B02... names), their units found from the values (reflectance 0-1 or x 10000; dB or linear backscatter), and a year of monthly composites made (each month the median of its observations; The series' own dates gives it up to 24 dates as they are), with each pixel's latitude and longitude. Two uses:

  • Make the embeddings: Presto's encoding of every pixel of the scope (128 values) for the year, written as an embedding layer that opens in the Embeddings panel like TESSERA's and AlphaEarth's (principal components, similarity, change).
  • Train: a classifier on the encodings (the encoder kept as pretrained, a linear head learning from your samples; Adam 1e-3, 50 epochs, as zeit.ai.train), applied as the others. Few samples suffice where the encodings separate the classes.

Janus's encodings are those of the authors' code to float32's precision (a few millionths; tools/presto_reference.py, crates/janus-ml/tests/presto.rs).

U-TAE (Garnot & Landrieu 2021) segments whole patches (32, 64 or 128 px a side, every date): a U-Net encodes each date, a temporal attention fuses them at the bottleneck and weighs the dates of every scale, so a pixel's class comes from its neighbourhood too (the edges of fields). It learns from dense labels: every pixel of the polygons of the sources above (or of the pins and points: one pixel each), or A class map (every pixel of a classification already on the map, e.g. a TempCNN's corrected), optionally only inside the ROI. Each band is standardized (its mean and deviation); a date without observation is left out of the attention. With the ten Sentinel-2 bands (B2, B3, B4, B5, B6, B7, B8, B8A, B11, B12, by name) it can start from the authors' PASTIS weights (20 crop types in France; 13 MB taken once from their Zenodo record, CC-BY-4.0), its last layer made for your classes. The image (or the visible area, or the ROI) is classified in windows overlapping by a quarter, each pixel the mean of the windows' probabilities. With the authors' weights, Janus's U-TAE gives the scores of their code (zeit.ai.utae, a port of it layer for layer) to float32's precision (tools/utae_reference.py, crates/janus-ml/tests/utae.rs).

TempCNN (Pelletier et al. 2019) and L-TAE (Garnot & Landrieu 2020) are written from their authors' papers and code, not from sits, and trained with the authors' settings. On sits' own samples (samples_modis_ndvi, samples_l8_rondonia_2bands), against sits with its defaults, the mean test accuracy over three seeds is:

samplesmodelsitsJanus
MODIS NDVITempCNN0.8700.877
Rondonia Landsat 8TempCNN0.6980.823
MODIS NDVIL-TAE0.8730.888
Rondonia Landsat 8L-TAE0.2290.833

sits' L-TAE reaches 0.229 on the Rondonia samples, which suggests that sits' own training failed there (a reading to take with caution: we ran it as a black box). tools/ml_sits_reference.R runs sits; the comparison is crates/janus-ml/tests/sits.rs. TempCNN and L-TAE models saved by earlier versions of Janus no longer open ("model from an earlier version of Janus: train it again"); Random Forest, U-TAE and Presto models open as before.

Field delineation (parcels)

Tools > Classification & pattern recognition > Field delineation (parcels) draws the fields of a Sentinel-2 series (blue, green, red and NIR, L2A digital numbers) as parcels, with the networks of Fields of The World (Kerner et al. 2025) and WRI's Trazo (Grupp et al. 2026): a U-Net (EfficientNet-B3) that labels each pixel of two composites of a season, window A about the green-up and B about the harvest, as background, field interior or field boundary. Ported to Burn from their published weights (CC-BY-4.0, downloaded once into Janus's folder), on the GPU or the CPU, no Python.

  • Model: Trazo3 (South America, best in Mato Grosso), Trazo SA (the soy ecoregions), Trazo2, Trazo1, FTW B3 (the world), or a .janusfields file trained in Janus (Open...). The Trazo networks read the composites as they are (as they were trained: upsampled, their pixel IoU in Mato Grosso falls from 77 to 55 %), FTW's upsampled twice, as ftw inference run does.
  • Season: found in the series (the area's NDVI date by date; each window ± days about its start and end, shown by Find the season) or two windows chosen; each window's median composite, the quality band applied.
  • Parcels: watershed (each field's sure interior, Seeds %, floods over the boundary's probability, so neighbouring fields touch) or interiors (FTW) (each set of connected interior pixels, as ftw-tools polygonize); a Minimum area (smaller ones merged into a neighbour) and a Simplify tolerance. Tiles of 128-512 px overlapping, each cut back to its middle.
  • Outputs: the class map, the interior and boundary probabilities, the parcels' map and their polygons (fields_parcels.gpkg: area_ha, perimeter_m, pixels, mean_interior), opened as a vector layer.
  • Train on your fields: a vector layer of fields drawn (or opened) in an area and an ROI around that area, where every field is drawn (in the ROI, pixels in no polygon are background and the polygons' edges boundary; outside it nothing is assumed). The chosen model is fine-tuned on chips of the ROI (its batch normalization frozen) for a number of epochs and saved in field_models/NAME.janusfields, chosen as the model at once.

On the Trazo dataset's test chips, scored as ftw model test scores them, Trazo3 in Janus gives WRI's published figures (pixel IoU of the interior 79.1 % in Mato Grosso, 75.3 % on the soy set, 68.1 % in Chiquitania; WRI: 79.2, 75.0 and 68.8; crates/janus-ml/examples/fields_eval.rs), and its scores are those of PyTorch's segmentation_models_pytorch within 1e-3 (tools/fieldnet_reference.py, crates/janus-ml/tests/fieldnet.rs). The watershed finds more whole fields than the interiors (object recall 36, 49 and 44 % against 25, 35 and 36 %). The guide: site/fields.html.

Spectra (hyperspectral)

A file whose bands carry their wavelength opens as a spectrum instead of a series in time: the chart's axis is the wavelength (nm), the time bar moves through the bands and each layer is labelled by its wavelength (650.2 nm). It works for any such file; EnMAP is the first case tested.

  • Wavelengths are read from the band metadata (ENVI's wavelength and wavelength units, nm or µm), from GDAL's CENTRAL_WAVELENGTH_UM, or from the METADATA.XML of an EnMAP product (its GeoTIFF delivery has none of its own). Bands are sorted by wavelength.
  • EnMAP: open the product folder, the folder its zip extracts to (the product in a subfolder) or its …-SPECTRAL_IMAGE file: the spectral image is opened alone, not the quality layers beside it. Example scenes (L2A, no registration): enmap.org/data_tools/exampledata; the whole archive is free with a DLR account.
  • On the map: a spectrum opens in true colour (bands nearest to 640, 550 and 470 nm) in the RGB composite mode; the composite list above the R, G, B sliders also has colour infrared, SWIR and agriculture. Value mode shows one band, the time bar choosing which (it starts at 860 nm).
  • On the chart: the spectrum of the cursor, the pins and the ROI (mean and p10–p90 per band). Bands without data (e.g. the water absorption bands, all no-data in EnMAP L2A) leave a gap, and so does a stretch of the spectrum without bands (EnMAP L2A has none from ~1760 to ~1940 nm). Other spectra open as layers are drawn on the same axis and follow the band shown.
  • CSV (copy the chart): a wavelength_nm column instead of date.
  • Index map (Display panel → Index map): NDVI, NDRE (red edge), NDWI, NDMI, NBR, NDSI or PRI from the bands nearest to their wavelengths, added as a layer of its own above the spectrum (dated by the scene's name, e.g. an EnMAP product's acquisition date).
  • Principal components and similarity (Display panel → Principal components, similarity, or the Embeddings panel): each pixel's spectrum is one vector, as embeddings are. Principal components (RGB): the first three of the whole scene, or of an ROI (ROI (local)), as red, green and blue. Similarity to a reference: the cosine of the angle between each spectrum and the cursor's, a pin's or the ROI mean (1 = the same shape, brightness does not count; the spectral angle of SAM is its arc cosine). Bands without data anywhere are left out; the view can be exported as a GeoTIFF at full resolution (Ctrl+Shift+M).
  • A series of scenes (one file per date, e.g. a folder holding several EnMAP products): dates from the names, each band named with its wavelength, and the Index by wavelength list in the Bands section. It opens in NDVI.
  • Every band in each block: a compressed GeoTIFF with every band in each block (pixel-interleaved, gdal_translate's default; a stack exported from Earth Engine) decompresses all its bands for any one of them. Janus reads it block by block, every date of a block at once, its blocks decompressed by Janus itself when DEFLATE or ZSTD without a predictor: the overview, an ROI and the exact series each decompress a block once (875 Float64 bands of 1690 x 1675, a CCDC stack of 3.3 GB, 125 dates of 7 bands: the overview in 5 s rather than over 15 minutes). Zoomed in, the first date shown at a place reads every date there at once (each block decompressed once) and keeps them in memory (an eighth of it at most, the places seen longest ago let go first): paging or playing through the dates there reads nothing more. The full-resolution cache of such a file is built block by block too, every date at once (the CCDC stack: 7 s rather than about two hours).
  • The Zeit tools work along time and are disabled on a spectrum.

Embeddings

Foundation models summarise each 10 m pixel and year as a vector: AlphaEarth Foundations (Google DeepMind; 64 dimensions, from optical, radar, lidar and climate data) and TESSERA (128, from Sentinel-1 and -2 time series). The values have no physical unit; what matters is how vectors compare: similar places have similar vectors.

Opening. A folder with one GeoTIFF per year and one band per dimension (what Janus downloads, or zeit.save_raster per year), a single GeoTIFF of one year with 16 or more bands, or zeit.save_raster's file of every year (bands <date>_A00...). Janus recognises them by Zeit's ZEIT_EMBEDDING tag or by their band names (A00, A01...), and opens the Embeddings panel. Zeit's change detection tools are disabled on them (an embedding has no seasonal signal), as Zeit itself refuses them.

Adding them over any series. In the Layers panel, Embeddings: pick the source, the years and the cell size (10 m native; coarser cells are the mean of the 10 m vectors), the visible area or the ROI, and Add embeddings. The size is estimated first (Int16, D values per pixel and year) and very large areas are refused. Janus downloads them itself, no Python needed, in the background (a bar on the map tells the year and the time left; Tools → Tasks has its log) and writes one GeoTIFF per year under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Janus\results\embeddings; the layer is added on top, reprojected if the series is in another CRS, while the series you were studying stays active. The first AlphaEarth download fetches its file index (78 MB, once a month).

Views (Embeddings panel):

  • Principal components (RGB): three components (PC1-3 by default; any of the first six) stretched between the 2 and 98 % percentiles. One PCA for every year, so a colour means the same in each year and playing the series shows real change. ROI (local): the PCA of the ROI's pixels only, applied to the whole map: the colours spread over the differences inside the ROI (e.g. the states of a forest that the whole scene's PCA spends on water vs. city). It is fitted again as you move the ROI (a few milliseconds).
  • Similarity to a reference: the cosine similarity of every pixel to the vector under the cursor (live, as the mouse moves), a pin, or the ROI's mean vector, in the year shown or a fixed year. The panel charts the similarity of the cursor and the pins over the years ("did this pasture come to look like the forest?").
  • Change between years: 1 − cosine similarity of each pixel's vectors in the year shown and the previous year (or a fixed year).
  • Band values: one dimension as an ordinary band, with every mode of the Display panel.

The panel also plots the latent profile: the D values of the cursor's and the pins' vectors. The status bar shows the components or the similarity under the cursor.

Saving a view (File → Export embeddings as GeoTIFF...): the view shown, over the visible area or the whole layer, as a Float32 GeoTIFF on the layer's own grid and CRS (no data = NaN), computed again at full resolution from the vectors in the files (not from the reduced copy on screen). Principal components: one band per fitted component (six), the scores along each one (not stretched), named with their share of the variance; Similarity: one band, the cosine similarity to the reference shown; Change: one band, the cosine distance between the two years. The model, year, reference and licence go in the file's metadata.

How it is computed. Every year is kept in memory at reduced resolution as Int8 with a scale per dimension (within the overview memory of Settings), its range taken from a sample of every year (0.1 to 99.9 %, widened by 5 %): every year fits it, not just one. The PCA takes up to 65 536 vectors: the covariance in parallel with SIMD kernels (AVX2 + FMA when the CPU has them, else SSE2; NEON on Apple Silicon), then the leading eigenvectors by subspace iteration. Measured (2026-10-10, 18 threads, AVX2): a PCA of 128 dimensions in ~10 ms (covariance 4 ms, 19 ms without SIMD), an image of a year of 1 Mpx in ~4 ms; reading 8 years of TESSERA (622 × 453 px, 480 MB of GeoTIFFs) in ~4 s. jn --selftest-embeddings prints these timings on any computer.

Vector layers

Field plots, samples of a map's accuracy assessment, forest inventory plots, parcels or burned areas usually come as vector files. File → Add vector layer... (or the Layers panel, a drop, the Files panel, the command line) reads them through OGR, which comes with GDAL: GeoJSON, Shapefile, GeoPackage (each of its layers becomes a vector layer), KML/KMZ, FlatGeobuf, GML, GPX and CSV tables of points (columns named x/lon/longitude/easting and y/lat/latitude/northing; without a CRS, coordinates within ±180/±90 are read as longitude and latitude).

  • On the map: in the drawing order of the Layers panel, with the series (a new vector layer on top; drag it under a series, or right click → Move, and the series covers it), on every map panel and the swipe, in any CRS (placed on the active layer's grid through PROJ, in parallel and in the background, again whenever the active layer changes to another grid: the map goes on meanwhile, the layer marked placing... in the Layers panel). Points are dots; lines and polygons (with their holes) are outlines. Each layer has a colour, can be hidden or removed; right click its name for Zoom to it.
  • Without a raster: vector files opened alone make a map of their own (an empty canvas in their CRS over their extent, with the basemap under them); it goes when a series is opened. The Time series and Statistics panels are left out until then: they come with the first raster series (where they were, if nothing else was moved) and go with the last one.
  • Large layers: the GPU draws them, as a GIS does. Once placed, a layer is uploaded once (in the background, a moment for millions of vertices) as levels of detail (each ring simplified with Douglas–Peucker, the tolerance doubling from 1/32 of a pixel) in pieces along a Morton curve; each frame draws the coarsest level within half a screen pixel of the exact outline, and only the pieces in view. The 5572 municipalities of Brazil (IBGE 2021, 16.9 million vertices) draw in about 0.3 ms a frame, the whole country or zoomed in to the street, against 45 ms (and an incomplete map) on the CPU; read in 0.5 s, placed in 0.05 s (0.4 s reprojected to UTM), built for the GPU in 0.4–1.2 s, 230–380 MB of GPU memory. A level is kept when it has at most 60% of the points of the finer one kept (counted on a sample of the pieces first, so only those are made); a ring smaller than a level's tolerance is a dot in it. A file is read whole up to 100 million vertices (about 80 bytes each once drawn). A state's CAR, made up (tools/bench_vector_draw.py: 1.2 million polygons, 34 million vertices, bench/vector-draw.json), is read in 1.6 s, placed in 0.4 s, built for the GPU in 1.0–1.3 s (730 MB on the GPU, 2.8 GB of memory in all: the memory freed by reading, placing and building given back; 4.9 GB before) and drawn whole 3–4 s after it was opened; a frame takes 4–9 ms with the whole layer in view, 1 ms 8 times closer, 0.4 ms zoomed in, and 97% of its outlines (as GDAL rasterizes them) are lit zoomed out, where the CPU drew 56% of a file cut at 20 million vertices. Until a layer is uploaded the CPU draws it (300 000 vertices a frame), and always the feature under the cursor, the one interpreted and those picked in the attribute table. The feature under the cursor (and Alt + click) is found through a grid of the features' boxes: 38 µs among those 1.2 million polygons (0.7 ms before).
  • Labels (the layer's menu → Labels): the values of a column (a field's name, a municipality, a CAR id...) written on the map, their size, colour and halo (an outline that keeps them legible over any image). A polygon's label at its point inside (the one Alt + click and the interpretation use), a line's at the middle of its length, a point's to its right. A polygon or a line is labelled only when its box on screen is at least twice the label's height; no two labels overlap: the larger features first (a polygon's box, a line's length), a label that would cover one already placed is left out, as are those of a layer under another's; at most 1500 a view. The column is read on a thread (OGR skipping the geometries and the other fields), the label points made once per placement in a grid of cells, each cell's features from the largest, so a view of a million polygons takes only those large enough. Kept in the project, copied with Copy style (a saved style too), drawn in the map's PNG and the animation (Pins, ROI and vector layers). --labels FIELD[,SIZE] labels every vector layer (screenshots).
  • Attributes: a file opens with its geometries alone (OGR skips the fields: 200 000 polygons of 16 fields read in 0.23 s from a GeoPackage instead of 1.07 s, 0.68 s instead of 1.85 s from a Shapefile); the fields are read when asked. Hovering a point shows its fields (read for it alone); for lines and polygons hold Alt. The status bar names the feature under the cursor.
  • Attribute table (right click → Attribute table, or View → Attribute table): the layer's rows in a panel next to the chart (below the map without a series), read from the file in the background the first time; a filter (a text in any field), a click on a column's header sorts by it (numbers as numbers; again: descending, then as read), a click on a row highlights its feature on the map, a double click zooms to it.
  • A polygon as the ROI: Alt + click it. Its holes are left out; the statistics, box plots, embeddings' local PCA and the scatter use the pixels whose centres are inside, on every layer.
  • The ROI's vertices edited (Shift+R, View → Edit ROI vertices): the ROI's polygon (drawn, or taken from a layer with Alt + click: the file is not changed) adjusted before it is used. Drag a vertex; drag the dot in the middle of an edge to add a vertex there; right click a vertex, or Delete over it, to remove it. Every change is a step of Undo (Ctrl+Z).
  • The ROI saved (View → Save ROI as vector...): a GeoPackage, GeoJSON or shapefile of one polygon in the active layer's CRS (fields name, layer, pixels), opened as a vector layer if asked; Alt + click on it gives back the same ROI, pixel for pixel. Read back by geopandas and burned by rasterio.features.rasterize on the grid, an outline of 600 vertices with a hole gives the same 5 146 615 pixels (tools/bench_profiles_vs_rasterio.py, bench/profiles-vs-rasterio.json).
  • Profiles of every line (right click a line layer → Profiles of every line...): each line, or each part of a multi-line, sampled about a pixel apart as the transect samples it (n = its length in pixels, rounded up, plus one, evenly spaced; distances in metres), through every date or a range of them, the values the chart shows. A task (Tools → Tasks, with progress and cancel, on the processing threads) that reads only the windows of up to 128 × 128 pixels around the samples, each once a date, and writes profiles.csv (a row per sample and date: fid, the fields chosen, part, sample, distance_m, x, y, col, row, date, value) and, if asked, profiles_wide.csv (a row per sample, a column per date). Against shapely (line_interpolate_point) and rasterio on 200 lines over 4096 × 4096 pixels and 12 dates (2 822 100 rows): the same pixels and the same values, float32 for float32, distances within 5 µm; 0.72 s with 3 threads against 3.6 s reading each date whole with numpy and 71 s with src.sample; the CSV written in 0.77 s against 9.9 s by pandas.

  • Extract series (right click, or the Extract series... button under the layer): the series of every feature at full resolution, as the chart shows them (band or normalized difference, quality mask applied), for the active layer or every visible layer, written as CSV in the background (Exports window):

    • points: the value of the pixel under each; polygons: the mean of the pixels whose centres are inside, with their count (pixels); lines are left out; a feature off a layer has empty cells for it;
    • a row per feature, a column per date (fid, the file's fields, lon, lat, then the dates; with several layers the columns are <layer> <date>), or a row per feature and date (layer, date, value), easier to read in R or pandas.

  • Interpretation (right click → Interpret..., or Interpret... under the layer; the Interpretation panel, next to Statistics): the features one by one, as TimeSync does with Landsat. The map goes to each one (zoomed in to at least the zoom on each setting; a polygon whole) and its series is on the chart: a point gets a pin, a polygon becomes the ROI.

    • N / Shift+N (or Page Down / Page Up, or the arrows in the panel): next / previous feature; Skip labelled goes to those without a label only; Next after a label moves on by itself.
    • 1–9: a label of the label set (Stable forest, Deforestation, Degradation, Regeneration, Agriculture, Pasture, Water, Cloud / no data, Other by default; edit it under Label set); 0 clears it.
    • D: the date of the change is the date on the map (go to it with ←/→ or a click on the chart); Shift+D clears it. Notes for anything else.
    • Shift+1 / Shift+2 / Shift+3: the label's confidence (low, medium, high). E adds another event at the map's date (the label chosen under Other events, else the feature's label): a point degraded, then cleared, keeps both.
    • Chips (Validation & uncertainty → Chips, or Chips in the panel): the feature at every date of the active layer, a small window around it in the map's colours (or its RGB composite), the feature's pixel outlined; one per year keeps the date nearest the map's day of the year. Click a chip to show its date on the map, double click to make it the date of the change. The next features' chips are read ahead.
    • The labels are saved a second after each change (in Janus' data folder, by file and layer): starting the interpretation of the same file again resumes it at the first feature without a label.
    • Export table...: the file's features with their fields and three more, label, change_date and notes, as GeoPackage, GeoJSON or Shapefile (with the geometries) or CSV (with lon, lat).

Validation: accuracy and area (Olofsson et al. 2014)

The Validation & uncertainty menu turns a map — a Zeit result (LandTrendr's year of detection, CCDC's breaks, a TWDTW or SOM class map...), a categorical layer at a date (MapBiomas), or any raster file — into a stratified random sample, interpreted point by point, and estimates of the map's accuracy and of the error-adjusted area of each class, with confidence intervals, following the good practices of Olofsson et al. (2014). A step-by-step guide with screenshots, from the strata to the report, is on the website: Validating a map, step by step.

Design (Validation & uncertainty → New sampling design; the Validation panel):

  • Maps to stratify: one map, whose classes are the strata, or several, whose agreement is (a stratum for each number of maps that call a pixel change: change in 2 of 3 maps...). Each map is read as classes (its values), intervals of its values (edges, e.g. -1, -0.1, 1 for a magnitude) or events (a date of change: > 0 is change, no data and 0 are not; with periods, e.g. 2000, 2010, 2021, a stratum per period). Tick the classes (or intervals) that are change.
  • Buffer: the pixels without change within N pixels of a change become a stratum of their own: omission errors (change the map missed) hide there, and a few points in it make the area of change much more precise.
  • Limit: every pixel, the pixels inside the ROI, or inside the polygons of a vector layer.
  • Compute the strata: one pass over the map(s) at full resolution in the background (another map is read on the first one's grid); the strata raster opens as a layer, with each stratum's pixels, area (hectares; on the sphere for a geographic CRS) and weight.
  • Sample size: from the standard error wanted for the overall accuracy (eq. 13, with the user's accuracy expected of each stratum), or given; allocation proportional, equal, Neyman or by hand, with a minimum per stratum (rare change needs 50–100 points). The panel shows the errors the design should give: the standard error of the overall and of each user's accuracy, and the interval of the area of change.
  • Draw the sample and create the project...: a GeoPackage (the project) and its strata raster beside it. The same strata, sizes and seed draw the same points. Later, Add points draws more in a stratum (still a stratified random sample).

The project (a GeoPackage: open it in QGIS, keep it with the paper): samples (the points at their pixels' centres, with the reference label of each), labels (every interpreter's labels), strata and project (the design, the maps assessed, the translations). Validation & uncertainty → Open project... resumes the work.

Interpretation: the sample opens in the Interpretation panel (see Vector layers), the map going to each point, its pixel outlined. Blind (on by default): the maps assessed and the strata are not drawn and the points are coloured only by their state (yours, others', disagreement, adjudicated), so the reference is not swayed by the maps. Labels describe the ground, not the map: the class, the date of the change, the confidence, other events, notes. They are written to the GeoPackage a second after each change. Mine to do lists the points you have not labelled.

Accuracy (updated with every label):

  • Reference labels → the map's classes: how each label reads for this map (guessed from the names; for a map of events, loss and disturbance labels are change); "can't tell" and clouds are left out. A point is change when any of its events is; with periods, by the date of the first.
  • The overall accuracy, the error matrix in points or in proportions of area (a click on a cell lists its points in the Interpretation panel: the errors one by one), each class's user's and producer's accuracy, and its mapped and adjusted area ± the interval (a chart of both).
  • As the labels came: the overall accuracy or a class's area as points were labelled, with its interval: label until it is narrow enough.
  • Maps of events: the agreement of the dates (within ± k years, the histogram of the differences) and the area of change by year with its interval, from the reference's dates.
  • Areas by the ... estimator: direct (the sample alone, Olofsson et al. 2014; Stehman 2014 when the strata are not the map's classes), difference (model-assisted: the mapped area plus the estimated net error, the share where the reference has the class minus where the map has it) or ratio (the mapped area times the estimated ratio of the two; needs points the map calls the class) (Stehman 2013; McRoberts et al. 2018). When the strata are the map's classes the three agree; when they are not (another map assessed with the sample, transitions, a buffer stratum) the model-assisted ones give narrower intervals where the map is good. The accuracies do not change with the estimator. The choice is kept in the project and used by the report and its Python.
