  • Transitions between two dates: two of the project's maps of classes (e.g. two dates of a categorical series): each pair of classes (Forest -> Pasture) is a class, its mapped area counted pixel by pixel inside the strata (in the background) and its reference read from each point's label and its dated events: the class at a date is the label, or the last event on or before it with one of the maps' classes (the dates are guessed from the maps' names, and can be typed). The table gives each transition's mapped and adjusted area ± its interval, user's and producer's accuracy (only changes hides the persistences); Python... gives the zeit.transitions code. The strata need not be the transitions: the points are weighed by the project's strata (Stehman 2014).

Maps: one sample assesses many maps. Add a Zeit result, a layer at a date or a file (Assess another map...): each is read at the points and its areas over the strata, and its labels translated; the estimators weigh the points by the project's strata (Stehman 2014), so maps other than the one stratified are assessed without bias. The table compares their overall accuracy, the user's and producer's accuracy of change and the area of change.

Interpreters: your name is in Settings (by default your login). Each interpreter can label a copy of the project (Save a copy for an interpreter...); Merge labels from a copy... brings their labels back (by point, the newer kept). The panel shows each pair's agreement and Cohen's kappa; Adjudicate... goes through the disagreements, and the label given settles each (the others' labels shown).

Report: Export the report... writes report.html (design, maps, matrices, accuracies, areas with figures, interpreters, a methods paragraph and the references; the transitions between two dates, when chosen, with transitions.csv) and a CSV of every table. Python... gives the zeit.accuracy (and zeit.transitions) code that computes the same estimates, by the same estimator, from the project's files.

Official alerts against a map of change

Validation & uncertainty → Official alerts... (the Validation panel's Alerts tab) compares a run's map of change dates (a Zeit result of this session that is a date: LandTrendr's year of detection, CCDC's, BFAST's or SCCD's break dates, CODED's change dates...; lengths of time, such as LandTrendr's duration, are left out), or a map of dates from disk (a single map open as a layer, or File...), with the alerts the agencies publish. A map from disk gives its dates in band 1 (0 or no data: no change) in one of four encodings, chosen under Its dates as or detected from its largest value: decimal years (2019.5; whole years, 2019, up to 3000), year and day of the year (2019183), YYYYMMDD (20190702) or days since 1970-01-01. It is not an accuracy assessment (the alerts are another map, with errors of their own; see the sampling design above for that); it tells where and when the two maps agree, and how late or early one is against the other.

Sources

SourceWhat it isHow Janus reads it
DETER (INPE)Polygons of deforestation and degradation seen in daily WFI/AWiFS images, dated (view_date) and classed (classname: DESMATAMENTO_CR, DEGRADACAO, CICATRIZ_DE_QUEIMADA, MINERACAO...)TerraBrasilis' WFS (https://terrabrasilis.dpi.inpe.br/geoserver/ows): deter-amz:deter_amz (Amazon) or deter-cerrado-nb:deter_cerrado (Cerrado), the map's box and window fetched in a task (Tools → Tasks) into a GeoPackage of the cache and opened as a vector layer (as Add web layer... does)
Any vector layerDated polygons (a date field, a class field optional)An open vector layer or a file
GLAD-L (UMD; Hansen et al. 2016)Landsat, 30 m (0.00025°), a pair of files per year and 10° tile: alertYY (2 probable, 3 confirmed) and alertDateYY (the day of the year, 1 = 1 January)UMD's public bucket, no key: storage.googleapis.com/earthenginepartners-hansen/GLADalert/C2/current/ (2021 to now), read over the network (/vsicurl/) for the map's box only; or files
GLAD-S2 (UMD's GLAD laboratory)Sentinel-2, 10 m (0.0001°), Amazon basin: alert (1 loss in the most recent observation only, 2 low, 3 medium, 4 high confidence) and alertDate (days since 2018-12-31)The same bucket's S2alert/alert/ and S2alert/alertDate/, no key; or files
RADD (Wageningen; Reiche et al. 2021)Sentinel-1, 10 m, the tropics: as GFW encodes it, one band confidence * 10000 + days since 2014-12-31 (2 low, 3 high)GFW's GeoTIFFs need a GFW API key: open them from disk. Of the map's area reads GFW's public map tiles instead (tiles.globalforestwatch.org/wur_radd_alerts/latest/default/14/x/y.png, zoom 14, about 10 m at the equator; at most 400 tiles) and decodes their colours: the day is R * 255 + G, the confidence B / 100 - 1 (gfw-data-api's date_conf_rgb_calc). The export of Google Earth Engine (Alert 2/3, Date yyDOY) is not read
Integrated alerts (GFW)GLAD-L, GLAD-S2 and RADD in one band: confidence * 10000 + days since 2014-12-31 (2 low, 3 high, 4 highest: two or more systems)As RADD (gfw_integrated_alerts; the confidence of a tile's pixel in its alpha, A >> 2: 1 low, 2 high, 4 highest)

GLAD-L's files of the years the window covers are paired by name (alert21_*, alertDate21_*); several tiles or years keep each pixel's earliest alert. The hover text of each product says where its files are.

Rules (the same in tools/bench_alerts_vs_python.py):

  • The grid is the map's. A polygon covers the pixels whose centres it holds (GDAL's rasterization, as rasterio.features.rasterize); where polygons overlap, the earliest alert holds the pixel. A raster of alerts is warped onto the grid by the nearest pixel, each pixel's centre projected exactly (gdalwarp -et 0: GDAL's default interpolation within 0.125 pixel depends on how the warp is read, and took the other neighbour at a few edges). Pixels outside the alerts' cover (a raster's tiles) are left out of everything.
  • A map pixel changed when its date (decimal years; Janus's: the year plus the days since 1 January over the year's length, to the nearest day) is in the window; an alert pixel when its alert's date is. The window is From and To (by default all dates).
  • Areas: of change in both, only in the map, only in the alerts (ha, a geographic CRS's pixels by their latitude); the share of the alerts' area the map detects, of the map's change the alerts confirm, Dice's coefficient.
  • Counts: an alert (a polygon, or a raster's patch of 8-connected alert pixels: its date the earliest, its confidence the highest) is detected when one of its pixels changed in the map; a patch of the map's change (8-connected) is confirmed when one of its pixels is an alert's. Polygons too small to hold a pixel's centre are counted apart.
  • Lag: the map's date minus the alert's, in days, at every pixel in both (positive: the map later). Median, mean, quantiles (5, 25, 75, 95%; numpy's linear), the share within 30, 90 and 365 days either way, and a histogram of bins of Bin days (30 by default). A map of whole years (LandTrendr's) is said: its lags count from 1 January.
  • By class: DETER's classname, or the raster's confidence: alerts, detected, their area, the median lag.

Layers and files: the agreement map (1 both, 2 only the map, 3 only the alerts; the Agreement colours) joins the Layers panel, and for rasters the alerts' dates (decimal years, as the map) too; the run's folder is RESULTS/alerts/NAME_TIME. Export CSV... writes NAME_summary.csv (metric,value), NAME_classes.csv, NAME_alerts.csv (every alert: its id, date, class, pixels and hectares, those the map changed, detected, its median lag, a polygon's own area), NAME_lags.csv (the histogram) and NAME_agreement.tif.

Command line: --alerts SOURCE[,KEY=VALUE...] compares once a map of change dates is there (a run of this session: --zeit NAME --zeit-run; a result opened with --layer is a layer, not a run's map): SOURCE is deter-amz, deter-cerrado, wfs/oapif (url=, layer=, date=, class=, name=), glad-l, glad-s2, radd or integrated (files=CONF;DATE;... or download=1 for the map's area); keys map= (part of the map's name), from=, to= (YYYY-MM-DD), tab=0 (the panel left closed). --screenshot waits for the comparison and its layers.

Compared with geopandas, rasterio, numpy and scipy (the same rules written with them): tools/bench_alerts_vs_python.py (conda run -n geo), results in bench/alerts-vs-python.json:

The real cases are the validation guide's place (16 × 13 km south-west of Novo Progresso, Pará; tools/make_tutorial_data.py): LandTrendr's year of detection on the NBR of the eight dry-season Sentinel-2 composites (2017-2024) against the alerts of 2019-2023. Times are the comparison alone, the median of 3 (the alerts already fetched: DETER's 98 features took 5.6 s, RADD's 48 tiles 41 s); the rasters' times are mostly GDAL's warp, the same on both sides. GFW's RADD tiles decoded by Janus and by Python from the same PNGs give the same values. The lags count from 1 January of LandTrendr's whole years, so their sign says little here; with a dated map (CCDC, BFAST) they are the delay in days.

Animation (GIF, MP4, WebM)

File → Export animation (Ctrl+Shift+A) writes the map over a range of dates as a timelapse, drawn exactly as the map shows it (layers, colours, detail tiles, basemap, results on top):

  • Dates: from / to (a range that ends before it starts plays backwards; on a spectrum, bands), a step (every n-th date) and the frame rate (the map's speed by default).
  • Resolution: 1× or 2× the map's size on screen (rendered at it, not enlarged).
  • Format: GIF (no extra software; up to 256 colours per frame, optional dithering), MP4 (H.264) or WebM (VP9) through ffmpeg. Janus uses the ffmpeg set in File → Settings → Video export, else one next to the program, else the one on PATH (winget install ffmpeg, apt install ffmpeg, brew install ffmpeg). Without it, MP4 and WebM are disabled.
  • Overlays: a large date stamp (top left, with the layer and display mode), the legend, a scale bar (ground distance at the centre of the view; needs a CRS; also available for PNG figures), pins, the ROI and the vector layers; the basemap's credit whenever it is shown.

While the frames are drawn a progress window keeps the view as it is (Cancel stops it); each frame waits for its date, its detail tiles and the basemap's. The date shown comes back at the end. Encoding continues in the Exports window (Ctrl+J); a cancelled or failed export leaves no file behind. If ffmpeg fails, the error shows its last lines (the full log is ffmpeg.log in Janus' data folder).

Performance

  • The first open of a cube builds a reduced overview of every date (in parallel on SSDs) and caches it in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Janus\cache (macOS: ~/Library/Caches/Janus); later opens read that one file. Each date is saved as soon as it is built, so closing Janus in the middle of a build loses nothing: the next open reads those dates from the cache and builds only the missing ones. The Performance panel shows startup, build and read timings.
  • Spinning HDDs are detected and read with a single sequential reader (two readers were measured to be 4× slower). While the overview builds on an HDD, pins, ROI and detail tiles wait, so the head is not pulled away.
  • On an HDD the first open is bound by how fast the disk can sweep the files: GeoTIFFs stored as 1-row strips must be read almost entirely, even for a reduced overview. Cloud-optimized GeoTIFFs (tiled, with internal overviews) or an SSD make the first open much faster.
  • On an SSD the first date of a new overview is read by every background reader together, rows split among them, and shown as soon as it is read; the other dates follow, several at once. 41 Landsat dates (7318×7329 Float32, LZW, 1-row strips): the first image after 0.15 s on an NVMe SSD and 0.36 s on a SATA SSD (2.3 s when each reader took a date of its own), the whole overview in 3.6 s and 14 s.

  • Full-resolution cache (.janusfull files next to the overview cache): every date in 64×64 blocks, each compressed losslessly (float bits as integers, difference with the previous pixel, byte planes, zstd), so a series reads one small block per date. Values are bit-for-bit those of the files (after nodata, scale, normalized difference and quality mask). Measured on Landsat NDVI composites on a 5400 rpm HDD (41 dates of 7441×7317 Float32, LZW, 1-row strips, 8.5 GB per tile):

    from the files (HDD)from the cache
    exact series (41 dates)250–500 ms cold, ~5 ms once read0.7–1.0 ms
    ROI 256×256 (41 dates)~2 s cold, ~1.3 s once read~21 ms

    Size: 6.3–6.7 GB per tile (1.37–1.41× smaller than raw floats; zstd alone gives 1.17×). On an HDD the first open builds it in the same read as the overview: the overview pass reads each date at full resolution, one thread streams the file ahead while four decode and compress, and the overview is taken from those rows; once a date is read the disk goes on to the next one while its last rows are decoded. 41 dates of 7318×7329 (7.7 GB) on a 4 TB HDD: both caches in 51–52 s, against 47 s to read the files alone. When the overview already came from its cache, the cache is built in a pass of its own (54 s per tile, bound by the disk). Each date is saved as it is built and used right away; a stopped build resumes.

  • The cache is on by default for series on an HDD; File → Settings turns it on for every series or leaves it to Build it now (per series). With the files on an SSD it matters less.
  • Disk cache budget: the overview and full-resolution caches share one budget, taken from the disk that holds the cache folder. Automatic (the default): a tenth of the disk, 8 to 256 GB (a 256 GB SSD: ~25 GB; a 4 TB disk: 256 GB); File → Settings sets one by hand instead. Either way a tenth of the disk (10 to 100 GB) is left free: as the disk fills up the budget shrinks and the least recently opened series leave the cache first; the open series' caches are never removed. Checked at startup, before each cache file is written, when a series is closed and every minute. A full-resolution build that does not fit is not started (the panel says why: the budget, or the disk's free space); one running when the disk fills up stops (Resume once there is room); an overview that does not fit is built in memory without being saved. The Performance panel shows what the caches take, the budget and the disk's free space. Basemap tiles keep their own limit (512 MB, cache\basemap).
  • Threads: on an SSD the background readers (overview, full-resolution cache) use the processing threads of Settings, at most 12, and exact series, ROI, tiles and the transect up to 4. On an HDD both are one reader whatever the setting (a disk decision); the full-resolution cache built with the overview decodes on half the processing threads (1 to 4). The Performance panel shows the counts in use.

Updates

Help → Check for updates... asks GitHub for the latest release and shows the version you use (also under Help → About Janus, with GDAL's), the new one and its notes. On Windows, when Janus was installed with its installer, Download and install downloads the new installer and Install now closes Janus, installs the new version in the same folder (for you or for all users, as before) and opens it again. Elsewhere, or from a build, Download opens the new package in the browser. Janus checks once when it starts (Settings: Check for updates when Janus starts); when there is a newer version, a notice says so and the right of the menu bar shows Janus X.Y.Z is out (you are using ...) and Update, which in the installed program downloads it at once (then Install now).

Settings

File → Settings... (Ctrl+,; Mac: Command+,). Everything applies at once and is kept in the layout file, next to the other data of Janus (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Janus\layout-0.7.ini on Windows).

SettingWhat it does
InterfaceModern (the default): the look of the image editors (Photoshop, Lightroom): the panels as rounded cards on a darker ground, their tabs on a darker bar, rounded controls, the selection in blue, soft shadows under windows and menus, and a proportional font (Inter); its themes are Photoshop's four greys, Darkest (the default), Dark, Medium and Light, picked from their swatches. Classic: Dear ImGui's look, as the C++ version draws it (its pixel font and the seven themes below). Everything else (the panels, their places, the menus, the shortcuts) is the same in both; --interface modern|classic[,THEME] chooses for one run
Theme (classic)Dark (the default), Light, Classic (ImGui's original colours), Janus (the program's colours: blue on navy panels, orange accents), Studio (mid grey with dark text and dark chart displays) Graphite (dark grey with a yellow accent) or Matrix (phosphor green on black). Status text and chart series are adjusted to stay legible on each; the map, its colour bars and exported figures keep their colours
Panels' backgroundHow opaque the panels' backgrounds are, 10 to 100% (100% by default): below 100% the desktop (or whatever is behind the window) shows through the panels, the menus and the map's empty area, while text, chart lines, controls and the map's data stay opaque; in every window, the detached panels' included. Contrast is kept on the theme's own colours
Whole windowThe opacity of the whole window, 20 to 100% (the system's window transparency: text and map included), and of every detached panel
Font sizeSize of the interface text, 10 to 28 px (13 by default: ImGui's pixel font in the classic interface, other sizes its scalable font; Inter in the modern one). Widths grow with the font (the fields, lists, buttons and sliders, in proportion to 13 px), texts that would not fit are cut short with an ellipsis (the whole on hover); exported figures keep their text as at 13 px
Files panel follows what is openedOn by default: opening a series, a file or a folder (from anywhere) expands the Files panel down to it and scrolls there; its folder is listed again, so new files show up
Reopen the last session at startOff by default. On: Janus opens with the layers, styles and view it had when it was closed (kept every minute and at exit, see Projects in Using the window); a session with changes not saved in its project is marked changed (*)
Check for updates when Janus startsOn by default: one request to GitHub when Janus opens; when there is a newer version, a notice and, on the right of the menu bar, the version and Update (downloads and installs it; Help → Check for updates... shows its progress)
Processing threadsHow many CPU threads Janus and Zeit may use, shown as N of M logical cores; default: all but 2 (at least 1), so the computer stays responsive during long runs. Applies to the readers of the open series (they shrink or grow at once), the full-resolution cache, exports (GeoTIFF compression, PNG) and Zeit: raster jobs started from then on (as OMP_NUM_THREADS, NUMBA_NUM_THREADS, the BLAS limits and Zeit's n_jobs; jobs already running keep theirs) and the process that fits the chart and estimates run times (replaced in the background once idle)
Downloads at onceHow many downloads (STAC series and composites, embeddings) transfer at the same time, 1 to 8 (default 2); the others wait their turn in Tools → Tasks
Overview memoryMemory for the overviews (1024 MB by default), shared by every layer open by their dates: 41 maps of one date each opened as layers of their own take what one series of their 41 dates takes. A single date has no statistics over time (nothing reserved for them). Apply reopens the active layer. --budget overrides it for one run
Disk cache budgetAutomatic (the default: a tenth of the disk holding the cache folder, 8 to 256 GB) or a size set by hand, 8 to 2048 GB; shows the size now, why it is smaller when the disk is filling up, and what the overviews and full-resolution caches take (see Performance). From an older version, a full-resolution cache budget changed by hand is kept; the old default (64 GB) becomes automatic
Clear overview cacheDeletes the cached overviews except the open series'
Full-resolution cacheWhen it is built (on demand, series on an HDD, every series), and clearing it (see Performance)
InterpreterThe name your labels of a validation project are kept under (by default your login), see Validation
Video export (ffmpeg)The ffmpeg executable used for MP4 and WebM animations (Browse...); empty: one next to Janus, else the one on PATH (see Animation)
